el-bacha-museum.name: Dar El Bacha
el-bacha-museum.tagline: Dar El Bacha is a stunning 1910 Marrakech palace showcasing Morocco's rich heritage, Moorish architecture, and the famous Bacha Coffee.
el-bacha-museum.p1: Built in 1910 as the residence of Thami El Glaoui, the powerful Pasha of Marrakech, Dar El Bacha ('House of the Pasha') hosted figures such as Winston Churchill and Charlie Chaplin during its heyday.
el-bacha-museum.p2: After decades of closure, the palace reopened in 2017 as the Museum of Confluences, displaying Islamic and African art alongside pieces reflecting Marrakech's Jewish heritage, all set among carved cedar doors, stained glass and zellige tilework.
el-bacha-museum.p3: One of the courtyards houses Bacha Coffee, a historic coffee house dating back to the same era, now serving over 200 varieties of Arabica coffee from around the world — access to the café requires a museum ticket.
el-bacha-museum.info3: Around 70 MAD for the museum (Bacha Coffee requires separate ordering inside)
el-bacha-museum.info4: Expect a wait for a table at Bacha Coffee — it's very popular
el-bacha-museum.desc: Dar El Bacha is a stunning 1910 Marrakech palace showcasing Morocco's rich heritage, Moorish architecture, and the famous Bacha Coffee.
el-bacha-museum.title: Dar El Bacha | Marrakech Travel Guide | MoroccoTripMap

jardin-majorelle.name: Jardin Majorelle & YSL
jardin-majorelle.tagline: A peaceful botanical haven famous for its cobalt blue villa.
jardin-majorelle.p1: Created in the 1920s and 30s by French painter Jacques Majorelle, this botanical garden is known for its vivid cobalt-blue villa and pavilions, set among bamboo groves, cacti and bougainvillea gathered from five continents.
jardin-majorelle.p2: The property was bought and restored in 1980 by fashion designer Yves Saint Laurent and his partner Pierre Bergé, and it now also houses the Berber Museum and, nearby, the Yves Saint Laurent Museum, dedicated to his fashion work.
jardin-majorelle.p3: It's one of the most visited sites in Marrakech, so tickets are sold online with a specific entry time slot, and it's worth booking at least a day in advance, especially in high season.
jardin-majorelle.info2: Daily, roughly 8:00/8:30–17:30/18:00 (last entry 30 min before closing)
jardin-majorelle.info3: Garden only around 170 MAD; combined ticket with the Berber Museum around 220–230 MAD
jardin-majorelle.info4: Book online in advance — time slots sell out, especially on weekends
jardin-majorelle.desc: A peaceful botanical haven famous for its cobalt blue villa.
jardin-majorelle.title: Jardin Majorelle & YSL | Marrakech Travel Guide | MoroccoTripMap

jardin-menara.name: Les Jardins de la Menara
jardin-menara.tagline: Marrakech's Menara Gardens is a historic 12th-century olive orchard featuring a large basin and a green-roofed pavilion.
jardin-menara.p1: Laid out in the 12th century under the Almohad dynasty, the Menara Gardens are built around a vast olive grove still irrigated by a centuries-old system of underground channels bringing water from the Atlas Mountains.
jardin-menara.p2: At the center sits a large reflecting pool facing a green-roofed pavilion added in the 19th century, once used by sultans as a summer retreat. On a clear day the pool mirrors the snow-capped Atlas peaks in the background.
jardin-menara.p3: It's one of the few large, free public green spaces in Marrakech and is especially popular with local families in the late afternoon. Compared to Jardin Majorelle, it's a more natural, rustic setting rather than a manicured botanical garden.
jardin-menara.info1: West of Hivernage, near Marrakech Menara Airport
jardin-menara.info4: City bus lines 11 and 12, or a 30–45 min walk from Jemaa el-Fnaa
jardin-menara.desc: Marrakech's Menara Gardens is a historic 12th-century olive orchard featuring a large basin and a green-roofed pavilion.
jardin-menara.title: Les Jardins de la Menara | Marrakech Travel Guide | MoroccoTripMap

jemaa-el-fnaa.name: Jemaa el-Fnaa & Souks
jemaa-el-fnaa.tagline: The beating heart of Marrakech, an open-air theater and labyrinth of artisan souks.
jemaa-el-fnaa.p1: Jemaa el-Fnaa has served as the main square of Marrakech's medina for close to a thousand years, and it remains the city's most famous meeting point. By day it is a fairly quiet mix of orange-juice stalls and snake charmers; from late afternoon onward it transforms into a lively open-air theater of musicians, storytellers, henna artists and acrobats.
jemaa-el-fnaa.p2: Once the sun sets, dozens of food stalls set up across the square, turning it into Marrakech's biggest open-air restaurant, with grilled meats, tagines, snail soup and fresh juices served late into the night.
jemaa-el-fnaa.p3: The square is recognized by UNESCO as a Masterpiece of the Oral and Intangible Heritage of Humanity, and it borders the medina's souks, where leather goods, spices, lamps and textiles are sold in a maze of narrow alleys.
jemaa-el-fnaa.p4: Bargaining is expected for souvenirs and for any photo taken of a performer, and it's wise to keep a close eye on personal belongings in the busier hours.
jemaa-el-fnaa.info2: Free, open-air, accessible at all times
jemaa-el-fnaa.info3: Late afternoon through evening, when the food stalls and performers appear
jemaa-el-fnaa.info4: 10–15 min walk from most riads in the medina; taxis stop at the edge of the square
jemaa-el-fnaa.desc: The beating heart of Marrakech, an open-air theater and labyrinth of artisan souks.
jemaa-el-fnaa.title: Jemaa el-Fnaa & Souks | Marrakech Travel Guide | MoroccoTripMap

koutoubia.name: Koutoubia Mosque
koutoubia.tagline: The minaret of this 12th-century mosque stands 77 meters tall.
koutoubia.p1: Built in the 12th century under the Almohad dynasty, the Koutoubia is Marrakech's largest mosque and its most recognizable landmark. Its 77-meter minaret is visible from almost anywhere in the city and served as the model for the Giralda in Seville and the Hassan Tower in Rabat.
koutoubia.p2: The name comes from the Arabic word for 'booksellers,' a nod to the manuscript market that once surrounded the mosque.
koutoubia.p3: As with all mosques in Morocco, non-Muslim visitors cannot enter the prayer hall, but the surrounding gardens offer excellent views of the minaret, particularly at sunrise or sunset.
koutoubia.info1: Avenue Mohammed V, near Jemaa el-Fnaa
koutoubia.info2: Exterior and gardens only for non-Muslim visitors; free
koutoubia.info3: Sunrise or sunset for the best light on the minaret
koutoubia.info4: A 5–10 min walk from Jemaa el-Fnaa
koutoubia.desc: The minaret of this 12th-century mosque stands 77 meters tall.
koutoubia.title: Koutoubia Mosque | Marrakech Travel Guide | MoroccoTripMap

medersa-ben-youssef.name: Ben Youssef Madrasa
medersa-ben-youssef.tagline: An ancient Islamic college and a jewel of Arab-Andalusian art.
medersa-ben-youssef.p1: Once the largest Islamic college in North Africa, Ben Youssef Madrasa was founded in the 14th century and rebuilt in 1564-65 under the Saadian dynasty. It could house several hundred students in its small cell-like dormitories, arranged around sunlit courtyards.
medersa-ben-youssef.p2: The star attraction is the central courtyard, paved in Italian marble and framed by intricate zellige tilework, carved stucco and cedar wood — a striking example of Arab-Andalusian craftsmanship.
medersa-ben-youssef.p3: Restoration work carried out in recent years has returned much of its original detail, and a short video on site shows the artisans involved in the renovation.
medersa-ben-youssef.info3: Around 50 MAD, purchased at the entrance
medersa-ben-youssef.info4: A short walk from Jemaa el-Fnaa and the Marrakech Museum
medersa-ben-youssef.desc: An ancient Islamic college and a jewel of Arab-Andalusian art.
medersa-ben-youssef.title: Ben Youssef Madrasa | Marrakech Travel Guide | MoroccoTripMap

palais-bahia.name: Bahia Palace
palais-bahia.tagline: A masterpiece of Moroccan architecture featuring painted ceilings and zellige courtyards.
palais-bahia.p1: Built in the late 19th century for the powerful vizier Si Moussa and later expanded by his son Bou Ahmed, Bahia Palace ('Palace of the Beautiful') spreads across nearly 8 hectares of courtyards, riads and gardens planted with orange and jasmine trees.
palais-bahia.p2: Inside, painted cedar ceilings, carved stucco and zellige-tiled floors showcase the craftsmanship of the period, and the marble courtyard surrounded by arcades is one of the most photographed spots in Marrakech.
palais-bahia.p3: The palace belongs to the Moroccan royal family but is open to visitors; plan for roughly 1–2 hours to walk through the main halls and gardens.
palais-bahia.info1: Rue Riad Zitoun el Jdid, Marrakech Medina
palais-bahia.info4: Arrive early to avoid tour groups and the midday heat
palais-bahia.desc: A masterpiece of Moroccan architecture featuring painted ceilings and zellige courtyards.
palais-bahia.title: Bahia Palace | Marrakech Travel Guide | MoroccoTripMap

palais-el-badi.name: El Badi Palace
palais-el-badi.tagline: Grand ruins of a 16th-century palace home to nesting storks.
palais-el-badi.p1: Commissioned by Sultan Ahmad al-Mansur after his victory over the Portuguese in 1578, El Badi Palace ('The Incomparable') was once decorated with gold, marble and cedar wood said to rival the finest palaces of the Islamic world.
palais-el-badi.p2: Much of that material was stripped away over the following centuries, leaving today's vast open-air ruin of sunken gardens and towering ochre walls, now a popular nesting site for white storks.
palais-el-badi.p3: Visitors can walk the main courtyard, climb the ramparts for views over the medina and the Koutoubia minaret, and descend into the former underground storage chambers. The pavilion also displays the 12th-century Koutoubia minbar, an intricately carved cedar pulpit.
palais-el-badi.info4: Bring a hat — the main courtyard is fully open to the sun
palais-el-badi.desc: Grand ruins of a 16th-century palace home to nesting storks.
palais-el-badi.title: El Badi Palace | Marrakech Travel Guide | MoroccoTripMap

tombeaux-saadiens.name: Saadian Tombs
tombeaux-saadiens.tagline: Richly decorated mausoleums with Carrara marble in the Kasbah district.
tombeaux-saadiens.p1: This royal necropolis dates back to the 16th-century reign of Sultan Ahmad al-Mansur and holds around 60 tombs of Saadian princes, along with over a hundred more graves belonging to family members and officials.
tombeaux-saadiens.p2: Sealed off and left forgotten for over two centuries, the site was rediscovered only in 1917 through an aerial survey. The main mausoleum's Hall of Twelve Columns, built with Italian Carrara marble, is the most celebrated room.
tombeaux-saadiens.p3: It's a compact site, so a visit of 30–45 minutes is usually enough, and it pairs well with nearby El Badi Palace and Bahia Palace in the Kasbah district.
tombeaux-saadiens.info1: Rue de la Kasbah, near the Kasbah Mosque
tombeaux-saadiens.info4: Arrive close to opening time to avoid the small entrance passage getting crowded
tombeaux-saadiens.desc: Richly decorated mausoleums with Carrara marble in the Kasbah district.
tombeaux-saadiens.title: Saadian Tombs | Marrakech Travel Guide | MoroccoTripMap

fes-el-bali.name: Fes el-Bali
fes-el-bali.tagline: The ancient heart of Fes, where souks, crafts, historic buildings and everyday life fill a maze of narrow streets.
fes-el-bali.p1: Fes el-Bali is the oldest and most atmospheric part of Fes, a vast walled medina where centuries of Moroccan history remain woven into daily life.
fes-el-bali.p2: Founded in the late 9th century, the medina grew into a major centre of learning, trade and craftsmanship. Its lanes lead past carved doorways, artisan workshops, food stalls and traditional riads.
fes-el-bali.p3: Allow at least half a day to explore the central medina. A local guide can help with orientation, while independent travellers may prefer to choose a few landmarks and leave time for wandering.
fes-el-bali.info2: Open-air medina; individual monuments have their own hours
fes-el-bali.info3: Free to walk through; some monuments charge admission
fes-el-bali.info4: Wear comfortable shoes and keep an offline map available
fes-el-bali.desc: The ancient heart of Fes, filled with souks, crafts, historic buildings and narrow streets.
fes-el-bali.title: Fes el-Bali | Ancient Medina of Fes Travel Guide | MoroccoTripMap

al-quaraouiyine.name: Al Quaraouiyine
al-quaraouiyine.tagline: A historic centre of Islamic learning and one of Fes's most important spiritual landmarks.
al-quaraouiyine.p1: Al Quaraouiyine is one of the defining landmarks of Fes and a symbol of the city's long intellectual tradition. Founded in the 9th century by Fatima al-Fihri, it developed into a major centre of religious scholarship and learning.
al-quaraouiyine.p2: The complex sits deep inside Fes el-Bali, surrounded by the dense fabric of the old medina. Its architecture brings together carved stucco, zellige tilework, cedar wood and elegant courtyards.
al-quaraouiyine.p3: Access rules can vary, and non-Muslim visitors should not assume that every part of the religious complex is open to entry. The surrounding lanes and nearby viewpoints still make it an important stop.
al-quaraouiyine.info2: Access varies; check current visitor arrangements
al-quaraouiyine.info3: Religious complex; visitor access may be restricted
al-quaraouiyine.info4: Explore the surrounding medina and nearby viewpoints
al-quaraouiyine.desc: A historic centre of Islamic learning and a major spiritual landmark of Fes.
al-quaraouiyine.title: Al Quaraouiyine | Historic Mosque & University in Fes | MoroccoTripMap

bou-inania-madrasa.name: Bou Inania Madrasa
bou-inania-madrasa.tagline: A Marinid masterpiece of zellige, carved stucco and cedar wood in the heart of Fes.
bou-inania-madrasa.p1: Built in the 14th century under Marinid Sultan Abu Inan Faris, Bou Inania Madrasa is one of the most celebrated monuments in Fes.
bou-inania-madrasa.p2: Its central courtyard combines zellige mosaics, carved stucco and cedar wood details, creating one of the finest examples of Marinid craftsmanship in the medina.
bou-inania-madrasa.p3: It is especially rewarding for visitors interested in Moroccan architecture. Take time to look closely at the geometric tile patterns and carved surfaces.
bou-inania-madrasa.info2: Usually open during daytime; hours can vary
bou-inania-madrasa.info4: Visit early for a quieter courtyard
bou-inania-madrasa.desc: A Marinid masterpiece of zellige, carved stucco and cedar wood.
bou-inania-madrasa.title: Bou Inania Madrasa | Fes Historic School & Architecture Guide | MoroccoTripMap

nejjarine.name: Nejjarine Museum of Wooden Arts & Crafts
nejjarine.tagline: A restored historic funduq celebrating Morocco's woodworking heritage and traditional crafts.
nejjarine.p1: The Nejjarine Museum of Wooden Arts and Crafts occupies a beautifully restored historic funduq in the heart of Fes el-Bali.
nejjarine.p2: Its collection explores Moroccan woodworking through tools, furniture, architectural pieces and everyday objects, giving useful context to the cedar woodwork seen throughout Fes.
nejjarine.p3: The rooftop terrace is a highlight, offering a chance to pause and appreciate the dense medina from above.
nejjarine.info2: Usually open daytime; closed hours may vary
nejjarine.info4: Allow about 1 hour, including the rooftop
nejjarine.desc: A restored historic funduq celebrating Morocco's woodworking heritage.
nejjarine.title: Nejjarine Museum Fes | Wood Arts & Crafts Travel Guide | MoroccoTripMap

chouara-tannery.name: Chouara Tannery
chouara-tannery.tagline: One of Fes's best-known artisan sites, where traditional leather tanning remains part of the medina's living economy.
chouara-tannery.p1: Chouara Tannery is one of the most recognizable sights in Fes el-Bali. From nearby terraces, visitors can look down over rows of stone vats used to clean, treat and dye hides.
chouara-tannery.p2: The tannery is part of a living craft tradition rather than a museum display. Workshops around it continue producing bags, slippers, belts and other leather goods.
chouara-tannery.p3: The experience can be intense, especially in warm weather. Take your time, compare quality and prices if shopping, and do not feel pressured to buy.
chouara-tannery.info1: Fes el-Bali, near the Chouara tannery district
chouara-tannery.info3: No standard museum ticket; terrace access may vary
chouara-tannery.info4: Warm weather can make the tanning area quite strong-smelling
chouara-tannery.desc: A living leather-working site and one of Fes's most recognizable craft scenes.
chouara-tannery.title: Chouara Tannery Fes | Traditional Leather Tanning Guide | MoroccoTripMap

bab-bou-jeloud.name: Bab Bou Jeloud
bab-bou-jeloud.tagline: The famous Blue Gate of Fes and a natural starting point for exploring the historic medina.
bab-bou-jeloud.p1: Bab Bou Jeloud is the best-known entrance to Fes el-Bali and one of the first landmarks many travellers see when arriving in the old city.
bab-bou-jeloud.p2: The gate stands at the beginning of Talaa Kebira and Talaa Seghira, important routes leading deeper into the medina. Cafés, restaurants and shops make the area lively throughout the day.
bab-bou-jeloud.p3: It is more than a photo stop: use it as an orientation point before visiting Bou Inania Madrasa and the central historic districts.
bab-bou-jeloud.info4: A useful meeting point before entering the medina
bab-bou-jeloud.desc: The famous Blue Gate of Fes and a natural starting point for the medina.
bab-bou-jeloud.title: Bab Bou Jeloud (Blue Gate) | Fes Travel Guide | MoroccoTripMap

mellah.name: Fes Mellah
mellah.tagline: The historic Jewish quarter of Fes, revealing another important layer of the city's heritage.
mellah.p1: The Mellah is the historic Jewish quarter of Fes, located in the newer part of the old city rather than deep inside Fes el-Bali.
mellah.p2: Its streets and buildings preserve a distinctive chapter of Moroccan Jewish history, with architectural details such as balconies facing the street and a more open relationship with public space.
mellah.p3: The quarter connects to heritage sites including the Ibn Danan Synagogue and the Jewish cemetery, making it a valuable addition to a broader heritage walk.
mellah.info3: Walking area; individual heritage sites may charge admission
mellah.info4: Combine with the Royal Palace area and Jewish cemetery
mellah.desc: The historic Jewish quarter of Fes and an important part of the city's heritage.
mellah.title: Fes Mellah | Jewish Quarter & Heritage Guide | MoroccoTripMap

marinid-tombs.name: Marinid Tombs
marinid-tombs.tagline: Historic ruins above Fes offering sweeping views over the ancient medina.
marinid-tombs.p1: The Marinid Tombs sit on the hills above Fes, overlooking the dense rooftops and minarets of the old city.
marinid-tombs.p2: The surviving ruins are associated with the Marinid dynasty, which made Fes an important political and cultural centre during the medieval period.
marinid-tombs.p3: The monuments are fragmentary, but the setting is the real attraction. At sunset, the hillside offers one of the city's memorable panoramic views.
marinid-tombs.info4: Paths are uneven; comfortable shoes are useful
marinid-tombs.desc: Historic ruins above Fes with panoramic views over the ancient medina.

outa-el-hammam.tagline: The lively heart of Chefchaouen, surrounded by cafés, restaurants and the red-walled Kasbah.
outa-el-hammam.p1: Place Outa el Hammam is the natural meeting point of Chefchaouen's old town, with terraces, cafés and restaurants facing the historic Kasbah.
outa-el-hammam.p2: It is an easy place to pause between walks through the blue medina, especially when you want mint tea and a little time to watch local life.
outa-el-hammam.p3: Use the square as a starting point for the Kasbah, nearby blue streets and the main shopping lanes of the medina.

chefchaouen_page.hero_subtitle: The Iconic Blue Pearl of Morocco Nested in the Scenic Rif Mountains.

overview.title: Welcome to the Blue Pearl
overview.p1: Chefchaouen is world-famous for its striking palette of blue-washed buildings tucked into the dramatic peaks of the Rif Mountains. Founded in 1471 as a fortress, this tranquil mountain town offers a peaceful retreat from Morocco's bustling imperial cities.
overview.p2: Wander through winding cobblestone alleys, relax in vibrant squares with mint tea, watch the sunset over the valley from the Spanish Mosque, or trek through the lush natural trails of Talassemtane National Park.

places.title: Top Places to Visit in Chefchaouen
places.subtitle: Iconic blue alleyways, historic kasbahs, and scenic mountain viewpoints.

outa.title: Place Outa el Hammam
outa.desc: The vibrant central square lined with outdoor cafés, dominated by the red-walled Kasbah and Grand Mosque.

kasbah.title: Chefchaouen Kasbah
kasbah.desc: A 15th-century fortress featuring lush Andalusian gardens, an ethnographic museum, and panoramic tower views.

raselmaa.title: Ras El Maa Spring
raselmaa.desc: Fresh mountain water spring outside the east medina gate where locals gather and wash rugs.

mosquee.title: Spanish Mosque (Bouzafar)
mosquee.desc: A hilltop mosque offering the ultimate sunset view over the entire blue medina and surrounding valley.

akchour.title: Akchour Waterfalls & God's Bridge
akchour.desc: Stunning river hikes, emerald pools, and natural rock arches in Talassemtane National Park.

haouta.title: Place El Haouta
haouta.desc: A peaceful square with a zellige fountain, perfect for mint tea away from the busy alleys.

babelain.title: Bab El Ain & Souks
babelain.desc: The main southern entrance to the medina leading to artisan workshops and local markets.

souika.title: Al Souika District
souika.desc: The oldest residential area featuring blue-washed cobblestone alleyways and carved doorways.

talassemtane.title: Talassemtane National Park
talassemtane.desc: Protected nature reserve with fir forests, dramatic peaks, and scenic hiking trails.

itinerary.title: Suggested 3-Day Itinerary
itinerary.subtitle: A relaxed schedule to capture the best photography spots and mountain landscapes.

day1.title: Exploring the Blue Medina & Sunset View
day1.desc: Stroll through the blue alleys, visit the Kasbah, enjoy tea at Place Outa el Hammam, and hike up to the Spanish Mosque for sunset.

day2.title: Akchour Waterfalls & Local Flavors
day2.desc: Take a morning grand taxi to Akchour for a scenic river hike, return for a traditional goat cheese tasting and rooftop dinner.

day3.title: Artisans, Relax & Ras El Maa
day3.desc: Walk along the Ras El Maa spring, observe local weavers, taste fresh mountain goat cheese, and shop for handmade products.
day3.duration: Half Day • Ras El Maa & Souks

directory.title: Find Your Ideal Stay in Chefchaouen
directory.subtitle: Discover charming traditional Dars, authentic Riads, and scenic mountain guesthouses.
directory.no_results: No accommodations match these filters. Try broadening your search.

eat.title: Best Restaurants & Cafés
eat.subtitle: Authentic Northern Moroccan dishes, goat cheese, and rooftop views

ssour.title: Bab Ssour
ssour.desc: Cozy multi-story restaurant serving home-cooked Tagines, fresh salads, and local specialties.

sofia.title: Restaurant Sofia
sofia.desc: Family-run eatery known for heartwarming pastillas, tajines, and friendly hospitality.

clock.title: Café Clock Chefchaouen
clock.desc: Vibrant cultural hub offering camel burgers, cooking classes, storytelling, and panoramic rooftop views.

morisco.title: Restaurant Morisco
morisco.desc: Prime spot on the main square for mint tea, breakfast, and people-watching.

aladdin.title: Restaurant Aladdin
aladdin.desc: Arabo-Andalusian palace offering panoramic Kasbah views from three rooftop terraces.

mandala.title: Mandala Pizzeria
mandala.desc: Wood-fired pizzas featuring local mountain goat cheese and fresh homemade pasta.

triana.title: Restaurant Triana
triana.desc: Charming riverside eatery blending refined Moroccan dishes with Spanish influences.

tips.title: Practical Tips for Visiting Chefchaouen

transport.title: Getting Here & Around
transport.desc: Reach Chefchaouen via CTM bus or private driver from Tangier (2h) or Fez (4h). The medina is car-free and best explored on foot.

shoes.title: Steep Alleyways & Shoes
shoes.desc: Wear comfortable walking shoes with good grip — the cobblestone steps and blue streets can be steep and slippery.

photo.title: Photography Etiquette
photo.desc: Always ask permission before taking close-up photos of locals, especially elders and children in the medina.

cash.title: Cash & ATMs
cash.desc: Most small shops, cafés, and local Dars only accept cash (Moroccan Dirham MAD). ATMs are available near Place Outa el Hammam.

daytrips.title: Best Day Trips from Chefchaouen
daytrips.subtitle: Discover waterfalls, national parks, and coastal mountain roads nearby.

akchour.title: Akchour Waterfalls & Bridge
akchour.desc: Emerald pools, river hikes, and the natural rock arch of God's Bridge (45 min drive).

talassemtane.title: Talassemtane National Park
talassemtane.desc: Trekking trails through fir forests, mountain peaks, and remote Rif villages.

tetouan.title: Tetouan Medina
tetouan.desc: UNESCO-listed Andalusian medina with rich artisan heritage (1h30 drive).

ouedlaou.title: Mediterranean Coast (Oued Laou)
ouedlaou.desc: Pebble beaches and turquoise waters of the Mediterranean coast (1h15 drive).

tanger.title: Tangier - Gateway to Africa
tanger.desc: Combine your journey with the legendary coastal city on the Strait of Gibraltar (2h15 drive).

review1.text: "The shades of blue at sunset from the Spanish Mosque were pure magic. A truly tranquil break from big cities."
review1.author: — Emma, UK

review2.text: "Staying in a local Dar in the high medina was wonderful. Fresh mountain goat cheese and tea on the rooftop every morning."
review2.author: — Marco, Italy

review3.text: "The hike to Akchour waterfalls was the highlight of our trip to Northern Morocco! Unspoiled green nature."
review3.author: — Carlos, Spain

q1.question: How many days should I spend in Chefchaouen?
q1.answer: 2 to 3 days is ideal to wander the medina, catch the sunset at the Spanish Mosque, and take a day trip to the Akchour waterfalls.

q2.question: Is Chefchaouen easy to reach by train?
q2.answer: No, Chefchaouen has no train station. The easiest options are CTM buses, grand taxis, or private transfers from Tangier, Tetouan, or Fez.

q3.question: Why is Chefchaouen painted blue?
q3.answer: Several theories exist: introduced by Jewish refugees in the 1930s symbolizing heaven, kept as a natural mosquito repellent, or maintained to keep homes cool and attract visitors.

q4.question: Are cards accepted in Chefchaouen?
q4.answer: Most small shops, cafés, and local Dars only accept cash (Moroccan Dirham MAD). ATMs are available near Place Outa el Hammam.

detailed_itinerary.day1_m: Morning — Place Outa el Hammam & the Kasbah
detailed_itinerary.day1_md: Start in the main square, visit the Kasbah and its gardens, then wander into the blue alleys while the light is soft and the streets are quiet.
detailed_itinerary.day1_a: Afternoon — Lost in the Blue Alleys
detailed_itinerary.day1_ad: Take your time in the medina’s lanes, stopping at small shops and cafés. Enjoy mint tea on the square and keep the camera ready for every corner.
detailed_itinerary.day1_e: Evening — Sunset at the Spanish Mosque
detailed_itinerary.day1_ed: Hike up to the Spanish Mosque for panoramic views over the blue rooftops at golden hour, then walk back down for dinner in the medina.
detailed_itinerary.day2_md: Take an early grand taxi to Akchour for a scenic river walk through Talassemtane National Park, with the Little Waterfall or the God’s Bridge trail if you have the energy.
detailed_itinerary.day2_ad: Head back to town in the afternoon and taste the region’s famous goat cheese, along with fresh bread and olives from a local vendor.
detailed_itinerary.day2_ed: Finish the day with a traditional dinner on a rooftop terrace overlooking the medina lights.
detailed_itinerary.day3_md: Walk to the Ras El Maa spring at the edge of the medina, where locals gather, wash and relax by the water.
detailed_itinerary.day3_ad: Visit local weavers and craft shops to see woven blankets, wool goods and handmade products being made, and buy directly from the artisans.
detailed_itinerary.day3_ed: Enjoy a last mint tea in the square before heading on to your next destination.

marrakech_page.hero_subtitle: The Ochre City of Palaces, Bustling Souks, Secret Gardens & Desert Gateways.

overview.title: Welcome to the Ochre City
overview.p1: Marrakech is a captivating sensory feast. Framed by the snow-capped peaks of the Atlas Mountains, this imperial city elegantly blends ancient Berber heritage with refined contemporary luxury.
overview.p2: Whether you are strolling through Yves Saint Laurent's Majorelle Garden, listening to storytellers at Jemaa el-Fnaa square at sunset, or heading into the Agafay desert for a night under the stars, Marrakech promises an unforgettable journey.

places.title: Top Places to Visit in Marrakech
places.subtitle: Iconic landmarks, royal palaces, and historic gardens you cannot miss during your stay.

jemaa.title: Jemaa el-Fnaa & Souks
jemaa.desc: The beating heart of Marrakech, an open-air theater and a labyrinth of artisan souks.

majorelle.title: Jardin Majorelle & YSL
majorelle.desc: A tranquil botanical haven renowned for its iconic cobalt blue villa.

bahia.title: Bahia Palace
bahia.desc: A masterpiece of Moroccan architecture featuring painted ceilings and zellige courtyards.

ben_youssef.title: Ben Youssef Madrasa
ben_youssef.desc: Former Islamic college and a masterpiece of Arab-Andalusian art.

saadian.title: Saadian Tombs
saadian.desc: Sumptuously decorated mausoleums crafted from Carrara marble in the Kasbah district.

elbadi.title: El Badi Palace
elbadi.desc: The majestic ruins of a 16th-century palace, serving as a sanctuary for storks.

jardin_secret.title: Le Jardin Secret
jardin_secret.desc: Restored palatial complex in the Medina featuring a traditional Islamic garden.

koutoubia.title: Koutoubia Mosque
koutoubia.desc: The minaret of this 12th-century mosque rises majestically 77 meters into the sky.

dar_el_bacha.title: Dar El Bacha
dar_el_bacha.desc: Dar El Bacha is a stunning 1910 Marrakech palace showcasing Morocco's rich heritage, Moorish architecture, and the famous Bacha Coffee.

jardin_menara.title: Les Jardins de la Menara
jardin_menara.desc: Marrakech's Menara Gardens is a historic 12th-century olive orchard featuring a large basin and a green-roofed pavilion.

itinerary.title: Suggested 3-Day Itinerary
itinerary.subtitle: A balanced plan to discover the essential sights without rushing through the city.

day1.title: The Heart of the Medina
day1.desc: Explore the iconic Jemaa el-Fnaa square, get lost in the artisan souks, and visit the historical Ben Youssef Madrasa.

day2.title: Palaces & Lush Gardens
day2.desc: Discover the majestic Bahia Palace, walk through the Saadian Tombs, and enjoy a peaceful afternoon at Jardin Majorelle.

day3.title: Modern City & Desert Excursions
day3.desc: Stroll around Gueliz district for art and modern dining, or head out for a sunset quad and camel tour in Agafay.

eat.title: Best Restaurants & Rooftops
eat.subtitle: Curated culinary experiences with top visitor ratings

nomad.title: Nomad Marrakech
nomad.desc: Trendy rooftop overlooking Spice Square, offering a reimagined local menu.

jardin.title: Le Jardin
jardin.desc: 16th-century verdant courtyard surrounded by banana trees, ideal for savoring a tagine.

fassia.title: Al Fassia
fassia.desc: Run exclusively by women, famous for its shoulder of lamb and pastilla.

moha.title: Dar Moha
moha.desc: Refined Moroccan gastronomy served around the pool of Pierre Balmain's former palace.

bacha.title: Bacha Coffee
bacha.desc: Legendary 1930s coffee room offering rare coffees and pastries in a lavish palace.

elfenn.title: El Fenn Rooftop
elfenn.desc: Stylish rooftop lounge offering panoramic views of the Koutoubia, creative cocktails, and tapas.

tips.title: Practical Tips for Visiting Marrakech

transport.title: Getting Around
transport.desc: Walking is best inside the Medina. For longer distances, take yellow Petit Taxis and always check the meter before starting.

bargain.title: Bargaining at Souks
bargain.desc: Haggling is part of the culture! Offer around 50% of the initial price and always keep negotiations friendly.

water.title: Stay Hydrated
water.desc: Marrakech can get very hot. Drink bottled water and enjoy the fresh orange juice at Jemaa el-Fnaa square.

daytrips.title: Best Day Trips from Marrakech
daytrips.subtitle: Rent a car, book a driver, or join a small group tour to reach these landscapes in a single day.

atlas.title: Atlas Mountains & Imlil
atlas.desc: Berber villages, valley hikes, and mountain views about 1h30 from Marrakech.

agafay.title: Agafay Stone Desert
agafay.desc: Sunset camel rides and dinner under the stars, just 30 minutes from the medina.

ouzoud.title: Ouzoud Waterfalls
ouzoud.desc: Morocco's tallest waterfalls and wild Barbary macaques, roughly 3 hours away.

essaouira.title: Essaouira Coast
essaouira.desc: Sea breeze, ramparts, and fresh seafood on Morocco's Atlantic coast.

review1.text: "Jemaa el-Fnaa at night was unlike anything I've seen — the food stalls, music, and energy were unforgettable."
review1.author: — Claire, France

review2.text: "Our riad in the medina was the highlight of the trip. Waking up to a rooftop breakfast over the rooftops was magical."
review2.author: — Daniel, Germany

review3.text: "The day trip to the Agafay desert was so easy to arrange, and sunset over the dunes with dinner after was worth every dirham."
review3.author: — Sofía, Spain

q1.question: How many days should I spend in Marrakech?
q1.answer: 3 to 5 days lets you explore the medina, palaces, and gardens at an easy pace, with a day free for the Atlas Mountains or Agafay desert.

q2.question: Is Marrakech safe for tourists?
q2.answer: Yes, Marrakech is a popular and generally safe destination. As in any busy city, stay alert in crowded souks and agree on taxi fares before you set off.

q3.question: What currency is used and can I pay by card?
q3.answer: Morocco uses the dirham (MAD). Cards are accepted in most hotels and restaurants, but keep cash for the souks, petit taxis, and small vendors.

q4.question: How do I get from Marrakech Menara Airport to the medina?
q4.answer: RAK airport is about 15 minutes from the medina. Official airport taxis, private transfers, and app-based rides are all available; agree the price before departing if using a taxi.

detailed_itinerary.day1_tab: Day 1 — The Heart of the Medina
detailed_itinerary.day1_md: Start at the Koutoubia gardens for soft light on the minaret, then walk into Jemaa el-Fnaa while the square is still relatively calm.
detailed_itinerary.day1_ad: Get lost in the artisan souks toward Ben Youssef Madrasa. Visit the courtyard if open, then continue through spice and leather lanes at your own pace.
detailed_itinerary.day1_ed: Return to Jemaa el-Fnaa as the food stalls light up. Try street food or a rooftop table overlooking the square.
detailed_itinerary.day2_md: Arrive early at Bahia Palace to avoid groups, then walk to the Saadian Tombs in the Kasbah district.
detailed_itinerary.day2_ad: Choose El Badi Palace for open-air ruins and storks, or book a timed slot for Jardin Majorelle and the Yves Saint Laurent Museum.
detailed_itinerary.day2_ed: Rest in your riad courtyard or book a calmer restaurant away from the busiest square edges.
detailed_itinerary.day3_tab: Day 3 — Day Trip or Free Time
detailed_itinerary.day3_m: Morning — Day trip departure or Menara
detailed_itinerary.day3_md: Leave early for the Atlas / Imlil, Agafay desert, or Ouzoud if booked. Otherwise visit the Menara Gardens for a slower local morning.
detailed_itinerary.day3_ad: Back in town, revisit favourite souk lanes, Dar El Bacha if open, or simply enjoy a hammam.
detailed_itinerary.day3_e: Evening — Last night in the Ochre City
detailed_itinerary.day3_ed: A final mint tea on a rooftop and an early night if you travel onward the next morning.

casablanca_page.hero_subtitle: Morocco’s economic capital where the world’s tallest minaret meets Art Deco boulevards and Atlantic sunsets.

overview.title: Welcome to Morocco’s White City
overview.p1: Casablanca is not the Morocco of postcard riads and snake charmers. It is a working, breathing metropolis of more than three million people, where Art Deco facades from the French Protectorate era stand beside glass towers, and the Atlantic crashes against the walls of the Hassan II Mosque. For many travellers it is simply the gateway, but those who stay discover a city of genuine character: excellent seafood, a surprisingly compact historic core, and a coastline that locals treat as their living room.
overview.p2: Whether you come for the breathtaking interior of Africa’s largest mosque, a sunset walk along the Corniche, or a day trip to the quiet capital of Rabat, Casablanca rewards curiosity. It is Morocco at its most contemporary — and still deeply Moroccan.

places.title: Must-Visit Places in Casablanca
places.subtitle: Iconic landmarks, coastal promenades and Art Deco neighbourhoods you should not miss.

hassan_ii.title: Hassan II Mosque
hassan_ii.desc: One of the world’s largest mosques, built partly over the Atlantic with a 210 m minaret. Non-Muslims can visit on guided tours.

corniche.title: Corniche & Ain Diab
corniche.desc: Casablanca’s 7 km oceanfront promenade lined with beach clubs, cafés and restaurants facing the Atlantic.

habous.title: Quartier Habous
habous.desc: A charming 1930s neo-Moorish neighbourhood with souks, cafés and the Mahkama du Pacha near the Royal Palace.

old_medina.title: Old Medina
old_medina.desc: A compact, authentic working medina with food stalls, spice shops and everyday Casablanca life — quieter than Marrakech or Fez.

place_mohammed_v.title: Place Mohammed V
place_mohammed_v.desc: The civic heart of Casablanca, surrounded by impressive Art Deco and neo-Mauresque public buildings.

ricks_cafe.title: Rick’s Café
ricks_cafe.desc: A loving recreation of the famous bar from the 1942 film, complete with piano, period décor and a refined menu.

villa_des_arts.title: Villa des Arts
villa_des_arts.desc: A beautiful Art Deco villa turned contemporary art museum showcasing Moroccan and international modern works.

marche_central.title: Marché Central
marche_central.desc: The city’s main market for fresh seafood, spices, flowers and everyday produce — a true slice of local life.

notre_dame.title: Notre-Dame de Lourdes
notre_dame.desc: A striking modern church famous for its huge stained-glass windows that flood the interior with coloured light.

itinerary.title: Suggested 3-Day Itinerary
itinerary.subtitle: A balanced schedule to discover the highlights without rushing your visit.

day1.title: Mosque & Old City
day1.desc: Morning guided tour of the Hassan II Mosque, then walk through the Old Medina and finish with sunset on the Corniche.

day2.title: Art Deco & Habous
day2.desc: Explore Place Mohammed V and the downtown architecture, then spend the afternoon in the atmospheric Quartier Habous.

day3.title: Day Trip or Coast
day3.desc: Take the train to Rabat for the Kasbah and Hassan Tower, or stay local and enjoy seafood and beach clubs along Ain Diab.

tips.title: Practical Tips for Visiting Casablanca

1.title: Getting Around
1.desc: The Casa Tramway is clean, cheap and useful for many central routes. For longer distances use red petit taxis (insist on the meter) or rideshare apps. The airport train is the easiest way from CMN.

2.title: Dress & Etiquette
2.desc: Casablanca is more relaxed than inland cities, but modest clothing is still appreciated, especially when visiting the mosque. Bring a light jacket — the Atlantic breeze can be cool even in summer.

3.title: Safety & Atmosphere
3.desc: Casablanca is a big city. Use normal big-city awareness, especially after dark in quieter streets. The Corniche and main tourist areas feel lively and safe in the evening.

el_jadida.title: El Jadida
el_jadida.desc: UNESCO Portuguese citadel and the famous underground cistern, about 1h20 by train or car.

mohammedia.title: Mohammedia
mohammedia.desc: Closest beach escape — clean sand, marina and seafood restaurants, only 25–30 minutes away.

azemmour.title: Azemmour
azemmour.desc: Quiet historic town with colourful street art and river views, often combined with El Jadida.

q1.question: How many days should I spend in Casablanca?
q1.answer: Two full days cover the main sights comfortably. Three or four days allow a relaxed pace plus a day trip to Rabat or El Jadida.

q2.question: Is Casablanca safe for tourists?
q2.answer: Yes. Like any large city, use normal precautions. Tourist areas, the Corniche and the centre are generally well-frequented and feel safe.

q3.question: What currency is used and can I pay by card?
q3.answer: Morocco uses the dirham (MAD). Cards are widely accepted in hotels and restaurants; keep some cash for taxis, markets and smaller shops.

q4.question: How do I get from Mohammed V Airport to the city centre?
q4.answer: The ONCF airport train is the most convenient option (about 35–45 minutes). Official taxis and private transfers are also available; agree the price or use the meter.

detailed_itinerary.day1_md: Book a guided tour of the Hassan II Mosque (non-Muslims outside prayer times). Allow time for the exterior esplanade and ocean setting.
detailed_itinerary.day1_ad: Walk or taxi along the corniche; cafés and Atlantic views without needing a full beach day.
detailed_itinerary.day1_ed: Dinner in the centre, Maarif, or near the marina — Casablanca eats late and urban.
detailed_itinerary.day2_md: Explore the old medina lanes and the edge of the working port area; keep expectations realistic — this is not Fez.
detailed_itinerary.day2_ad: Visit the Habous quarter for architecture and shopping, then Art Deco façades in the centre ville.
detailed_itinerary.day2_ed: Maarif or Gauthier for a contemporary Casablanca night out.
detailed_itinerary.day3_md: Museum of the History of Morocco or the cathedral exterior, depending on interests and opening hours.
detailed_itinerary.day3_ad: Easy ONCF trip to Rabat for the Kasbah and Hassan complex if you want a capital contrast.
detailed_itinerary.day3_ed: Casablanca is a hub — evening trains, airport transfers, or a last corniche walk.

seo.title: Fes Travel Guide | Medina, Riads & Things to Do | MoroccoTripMap
seo.description: Plan your trip to Fes: explore the ancient medina, Al Quaraouiyine, Bou Inania Madrasa, traditional crafts, Fassi food, riads, hotels, day trips and practical travel tips.
seo.og_title: Fes Travel Guide | Medina, Riads & Day Trips | MoroccoTripMap
seo.og_description: Discover the best places to visit, riads and hotels, food, a 3-day itinerary and easy day trips from Fes.

fes_page.hero_subtitle: Morocco's Spiritual Heart — a Living Medina of Crafts, History, Flavours & Centuries of Tradition.

overview.title: Welcome to Fes, Morocco's Cultural Capital
overview.p1: Fes feels different from the moment you enter its old city. Inside Fes el-Bali, one of the world's great medieval urban areas, narrow lanes open onto quiet courtyards, neighbourhood shops, artisan workshops and centuries-old buildings. It is a city to explore slowly, with no need to tick every sight off a list.
overview.p2: A trip to Fes is as much about atmosphere as monuments. Spend the morning discovering historic madrasas, stop for a plate of fragrant tagine, watch craftsmen at work, then return to a traditional riad before heading out again in the evening. If you want to understand Morocco's history, architecture, crafts and food in one place, Fes is a natural stop on your itinerary.

places.title: Must-Visit Places in Fes
places.subtitle: Historic schools, artisan quarters, viewpoints and quiet corners that reveal the character of Morocco's oldest imperial city.

fes_el_bali.title: Fes el-Bali
fes_el_bali.desc: The maze-like old city where souks, mosques, workshops and historic houses come together.

al_quaraouiyine.title: Al Quaraouiyine
al_quaraouiyine.desc: A historic centre of learning and one of the city's most important spiritual landmarks.

bou_inania.title: Bou Inania Madrasa
bou_inania.desc: Zellige, carved stucco and cedar details make this one of Fes's standout historic buildings.

nejjarine.title: Nejjarine Museum
nejjarine.desc: A beautifully restored funduq celebrating Morocco's woodworking heritage and traditional crafts.

chouara.title: Chouara Tannery
chouara.desc: One of Fes's best-known craft scenes, where leatherworking remains part of the medina's living economy.

bab_bou_jeloud.title: Bab Bou Jeloud
bab_bou_jeloud.desc: The famous blue gate is a natural starting point for exploring the old medina.

mellah.title: Fes Mellah
mellah.desc: Discover another layer of Fes through its historic Jewish quarter and surrounding royal district.

marinid_tombs.title: Marinid Tombs Viewpoint
marinid_tombs.desc: Come around sunset for one of the most memorable panoramic views over the medina.

itinerary.title: A Relaxed 3-Day Fes Itinerary
itinerary.subtitle: A simple first-timer route that leaves room for getting lost in the medina.

day1.title: The Heart of the Medina
day1.desc: Start at Bab Bou Jeloud, explore the quieter morning lanes, visit Bou Inania Madrasa and continue through the souks toward the Nejjarine area. Finish with tea on a rooftop overlooking the medina.

day2.title: History, Learning & Crafts
day2.desc: Explore the area around Al Quaraouiyine, then discover the traditional tanneries, leather workshops and Nejjarine Museum before enjoying a slow Moroccan dinner.

day3.title: Choose a Day Trip
day3.desc: Choose Volubilis and Moulay Idriss for history, Meknes for imperial architecture, or Ifrane and the Middle Atlas for a change of scenery. Return to Fes for a final rooftop tea.

eat.title: What to Eat in Fes
eat.subtitle: Fes is a rewarding city for food lovers, from simple medina kitchens to polished Moroccan dining rooms.

fassi.title: Traditional Fassi Dishes
fassi.desc: Look for pastilla, slow-cooked tagines, harira and seasonal salads. Fassi cooking is known for its balance of sweet, savoury and fragrant spices.

medina.title: Medina Food Stops
medina.desc: Follow your appetite through the medina: bakeries, soup counters, grilled meats, olives, dates and fresh juices make excellent informal stops.

rooftop.title: Rooftop Tea
rooftop.desc: Choose a rooftop terrace overlooking the old city and order mint tea alongside a traditional Moroccan dinner.

cooking.title: Cooking Experiences
cooking.desc: A local cooking class or market visit is a fun way to understand the ingredients and techniques behind Moroccan home cooking.

sweets.title: Moroccan Pastries
sweets.desc: Try chebakia, almond-based sweets and other Moroccan pastries with coffee or mint tea.

order.title: What to Order
order.desc: If it is your first visit, ask your host or server what is freshly prepared that day. Fes rewards curiosity more than a fixed checklist.

tips.title: Practical Tips for Visiting Fes
tips.subtitle: A few small details can make your first days in the medina much easier.

shoes.title: Wear Comfortable Shoes
shoes.desc: The old city is best explored on foot. Expect uneven paving, steps and plenty of walking.

stay.title: Stay Inside or Near the Medina
stay.desc: A riad gives you a more immersive experience, while staying just outside the medina can be easier if you prefer taxis and wider roads.

guide.title: Use a Local Guide if You Want Context
guide.desc: Fes has many layers of history and a guide can add context, especially on a first visit. If you go independently, save your accommodation location offline.

cash.title: Carry Some Cash
cash.desc: Keep Moroccan dirhams for small purchases, cafés, taxis and market stalls even if your hotel or larger restaurant accepts cards.

daytrips.title: Best Day Trips from Fes
daytrips.subtitle: Fes is a useful base for exploring the history and landscapes of northern and central Morocco.

volubilis.title: Volubilis
volubilis.desc: Explore Roman ruins, mosaics and open landscapes at one of Morocco's best-known archaeological sites.

moulay_idriss.title: Moulay Idriss
moulay_idriss.desc: A hillside pilgrimage town with whitewashed streets and views across the surrounding countryside.

meknes.title: Meknes
meknes.desc: Combine your Fes stay with another imperial city, known for monumental gates and historic architecture.

ifrane.title: Ifrane & Middle Atlas
ifrane.desc: Head into the Middle Atlas for cedar forests, cooler air and a completely different landscape from the medina.

q1.question: How many days should I spend in Fes?
q1.answer: Two full days can cover the main sights, but three days gives you time to explore the medina without rushing and add a nearby day trip.

q2.question: Is Fes a good destination for a first trip to Morocco?
q2.answer: Yes, especially if you are interested in history, architecture, crafts and Moroccan food. The medina is intense and busy, so a slower pace makes the experience easier.

q3.question: What is the best area to stay in Fes?
q3.answer: Stay in or near Fes el-Bali if you want atmosphere and easy access to historic sights. Ville Nouvelle is more convenient if you prefer modern hotels, wider roads and easier vehicle access.

q4.question: Can I visit the Fes medina without a guide?
q4.answer: You can explore independently, although the medina is large and easy to navigate imperfectly. A guide can be useful when you want deeper historical context or help discovering less obvious places.

q5.question: What should I eat in Fes?
q5.answer: Try Fassi specialities such as pastilla and traditional tagines, along with Moroccan salads, soups, pastries and mint tea. Ask locally what is fresh that day.

q6.question: What are the best day trips from Fes?
q6.answer: Volubilis, Moulay Idriss, Meknes and Ifrane are among the easiest additions to a Fes itinerary, depending on whether you prefer archaeology, history or nature.

detailed_itinerary.day1_m: Morning — Start at Bab Bou Jeloud
detailed_itinerary.day1_md: Enter the medina early while the lanes are calmer. Follow the main streets towards the historic heart, stopping at small bakeries, spice shops and artisan stalls along the way.
detailed_itinerary.day1_ad: Visit Bou Inania Madrasa and continue through the souks toward the Nejjarine area. Take your time rather than trying to cover every lane.
detailed_itinerary.day1_ed: Head to a rooftop for tea and a view over the rooftops, then enjoy dinner in or around the medina.
detailed_itinerary.day2_md: Visit a tannery viewpoint early for the classic colourful pits, then explore nearby craft streets.
detailed_itinerary.day2_ad: Walk toward Al Quaraouiyine and the surrounding lanes; visit Nejjarine Museum of Wooden Arts if open.
detailed_itinerary.day2_ed: A quieter dinner in your riad or a recommended Fassi kitchen — pastilla if you find it.
detailed_itinerary.day3_md: Leave early for Volubilis and Moulay Idriss, or Meknes, depending on your booking.
detailed_itinerary.day3_ad: Explore the ruins or imperial gates, then return to Fes by late afternoon.
detailed_itinerary.day3_ed: A final stroll near Bab Bou Jeloud or a rooftop view before onward travel.

q1.question: When's the best time to go?
q1.answer: Honestly, spring and autumn win almost every time — March to May or September to November, warm enough for the desert without being brutal in the cities. Summer works fine on the coast; it's really the interior and the south that get punishing.

q2.question: Will I need a visa?
q2.answer: If you're coming from the EU, UK, US, Canada or most of Latin America, no — you get 90 days visa-free on arrival. Rules do shift though, so it's worth a quick check for your passport before booking flights.

q3.question: How long should I actually spend in Marrakech?
q3.answer: Three or four full days is the sweet spot — enough for the medina, a palace or two, and a slower morning without feeling like you're racing the clock. Add a day trip into the Atlas or the Agafay desert if you've got the time.

q4.question: Is it safe to explore on your own?
q4.answer: Yes — most people travel around Morocco independently without any issues. Use the same common sense you would in any busy city: keep an eye on your bag in the souks, and settle the taxi fare before you get in, not after.

intro.text: MoroccoTripMap started because too many "best of Morocco" lists were clearly written by people who never left their desk. Everything here — from riads to desert camps — comes from actual time spent in more than 20 Moroccan cities, checked and rechecked so the details still hold up when you get there. It's all here in English, French, Spanish and Arabic, because a good recommendation shouldn't depend on which language you happen to speak.

el_bacha_museum_page.name: Dar El Bacha
el_bacha_museum_page.hero_subtitle: A 1910 pasha's palace, a museum of confluences and a very famous coffee house.

overview.title: The Pasha's House, Now a Museum
overview.p1: Dar El Bacha ('House of the Pasha') was built in 1910 as the residence of Thami El Glaoui, the powerful Pasha of Marrakech, and hosted figures such as Winston Churchill and Charlie Chaplin in its heyday. After decades of closure, it reopened in 2017 as the Museum of Confluences.
overview.p2: Inside, Islamic and African art sits alongside pieces reflecting Marrakech's Jewish heritage, among carved cedar doors, stained glass and zellige. One courtyard houses Bacha Coffee, now serving over 200 varieties of Arabica. Expect a wait for a table, and note that café access requires a museum ticket.

2.title: Timing
2.desc: Open daily except Monday, roughly 9:00 or 9:30 to 18:00 or 19:00. Go on a weekday morning to shorten the wait for Bacha Coffee.

3.title: Good to Know
3.desc: The museum ticket is around 70 MAD, and café access requires it. You order and pay separately inside for the coffee.

q2.question: How long do you need at Dar El Bacha?

seo.title: Jardin Majorelle, Marrakech: Tickets, Best Time & Visitor Tips | MoroccoTripMap
seo.description: Planning a visit to Jardin Majorelle in Marrakech? Ticket tips, best time to go, what to see in the blue villa and garden, and how to get there from the medina.
seo.og_title: Jardin Majorelle, Marrakech: Tickets, Best Time & Visitor Tips
seo.og_description: Yves Saint Laurent's cobalt-blue garden in Marrakech: what to see, when to go and how to skip the queue.

majorelle_page.name: Jardin Majorelle
majorelle_page.hero_subtitle: A small garden with a very big personality: cactus, bamboo and a blue you won't forget.

overview.title: A Painter's Garden, Saved by a Fashion Designer
overview.p1: After the noise of the medina, Jardin Majorelle feels like stepping into a different city. The French painter Jacques Majorelle began shaping this garden in the 1920s, filling it with cacti, palms and bamboo, and painting his studio in the intense cobalt blue that now carries his name.
overview.p2: Decades later the property was falling into neglect, and in 1980 Yves Saint Laurent and Pierre Bergé bought it and brought it back to life. Saint Laurent had been coming to Marrakech for years and treated the garden as a private refuge. It is easy to see why.
overview.p3: It is compact, so don't expect a sprawling park. What you get is a well-composed walk: shaded paths, bright pots against blue walls, still water and a lot of good photo corners. Go with a slow pace and it is one of the most relaxing hours you can spend in Marrakech.

gallery.title: Jardin Majorelle in Pictures
gallery.subtitle: A quick walk through the blue villa, the cactus beds and the water gardens.

s1.caption: The cobalt-blue villa framed by cacti and palms

s2.caption: Bamboo alley and shaded paths inside the garden

s3.caption: Blue pots and yellow accents against the Majorelle blue walls

s4.caption: Water basin with lily pads and papyrus

s5.caption: The Yves Saint Laurent memorial in the garden

moods.title: What to See at Jardin Majorelle
moods.subtitle: Three things worth slowing down for.

1.title: Cactus, Bamboo and Water
1.desc: Follow the paths under palms and bamboo, past oversized cacti and small pools. Look for the blue pots and yellow accents, they are what makes the colours pop.

2.title: Berber Museum in the Blue House
2.desc: The painter's former studio now holds a collection of Amazigh (Berber) jewellery, textiles and everyday objects. It is small and well displayed, and gives useful context for what you will see in the souks.

3.title: The Yves Saint Laurent Museum
3.desc: A separate building just outside the garden, focused on the designer's work and his Marrakech connection. Fashion fans will want a full hour here; everyone else can skip it without guilt.

plan.title: How to Plan Your Visit
plan.li1: Book a timed ticket online to skip the longest queues, and check opening hours on the official site, as they change by season.
plan.li2: Arrive at opening or in the last hour for softer light and fewer people.
plan.li3: Wear comfortable shoes and bring a hat and water; paths are shaded but the sun is strong.
plan.li4: Combine it with a wander through Guéliz for lunch, as it pairs better with the modern city than with the medina.
plan.p1: Tripods, drones and large bags are usually restricted, so travel light.

tips.title: Practical Tips for Visiting Jardin Majorelle

1.title: Getting There
1.desc: From the medina, take a petit taxi (about 15 to 20 minutes) and ask for the meter. Taxis wait outside the gate for the return, or book a driver ahead if you prefer.

2.title: Timing
2.desc: Spring and autumn are the busiest seasons. If you can only go at midday, expect a queue without an advance ticket and warm weather on the paths.

3.title: Stay Cool
3.desc: Summer heat is real. Go early, carry water and take a break in the garden café, which is a pleasant place for mint tea after the walk.

q1.question: Do I need to book Jardin Majorelle tickets in advance?
q1.answer: It is strongly recommended. The garden limits visitor numbers, and queues at the gate can be long, especially in spring and around midday. Buying a timed ticket online before you go usually saves you a wait.

q2.question: How long do you need at Jardin Majorelle?
q2.answer: About 1 to 1.5 hours for the garden alone. Add another hour if you also visit the Berber Museum inside the blue villa or the neighbouring Yves Saint Laurent Museum, and a little more for a coffee.

q3.question: When is the best time to visit Jardin Majorelle?
q3.answer: Right at opening, or in the last hour before closing. You get softer light, fewer people in your photos and cooler temperatures. Weekdays are calmer than weekends.

q4.question: Is Jardin Majorelle worth visiting?
q4.answer: If you like gardens, design or fashion history, yes. It is small, so it suits a relaxed morning rather than a full day. If you have only one day in Marrakech and love the medina, you may prefer to prioritise the palaces and souks.

q5.question: How do I get from the medina to Jardin Majorelle?
q5.answer: It is in the Guéliz district, about 15 to 20 minutes by petit taxi from Jemaa el-Fnaa. Ask for the meter, and note that taxis wait outside the entrance for the return.

jardin_menara_page.hero_subtitle: An old olive grove, a big reflecting pool and the Atlas on the horizon.

overview.title: A Calm Green Space Outside the Medina
overview.p1: The Menara Gardens were laid out in the 12th century under the Almohad dynasty around a vast olive grove, still irrigated by a centuries-old system of underground channels bringing water from the Atlas Mountains.
overview.p2: At the centre, a large reflecting pool faces a green-roofed pavilion added in the 19th century as a sultans' retreat. On a clear day it mirrors the snow-capped Atlas. It's one of the few big free green spaces in Marrakech, and more rustic than a manicured garden. Locals come in the late afternoon, and so should you.

1.title: The Reflecting Pool
1.desc: The classic view: pavilion, water and, on a clear day, the snowy Atlas behind. Sunset is when it looks best.

2.title: The Olive Grove
2.desc: Walk the shaded rows and see the old irrigation channels that still feed the trees. It's the quiet side of the gardens.

3.title: The Green-Roofed Pavilion
3.desc: Added in the 19th century as a sultans' summer retreat. Check locally whether the upper terrace is open on the day you visit.

tips.title: Practical Tips for Visiting Menara Gardens

1.title: Getting There
1.desc: The gardens are west of Hivernage, near Marrakech Menara Airport. City bus lines 11 and 12 go there, or take a petit taxi and ask for the meter.

2.title: Timing
2.desc: Open daily, roughly 8:00 to 18:00 or 19:00, depending on the season. Go for the last two hours before sunset, when the light is soft and locals arrive.

3.title: Good to Know
3.desc: The grounds are free, so there's no ticket to book. Bring water and a hat, as shade is limited around the pool.

q1.answer: The grounds are free to enter. Check locally, as access to the pavilion itself can vary.

q2.question: What is the best time to visit the Menara Gardens?
q2.answer: The last two hours before sunset, when the light is softest and the Atlas is clear if the weather is good.

seo.title: Jemaa el-Fnaa, Marrakech: Night Market, Food Stalls & Visitor Tips | MoroccoTripMap
seo.description: Visiting Jemaa el-Fnaa in Marrakech? Best time to go, what to eat at the night food stalls, rooftop views, safety tips and how long to stay.
seo.og_title: Jemaa el-Fnaa, Marrakech: Night Market, Food Stalls & Visitor Tips
seo.og_description: What to see, eat and expect at Marrakech's legendary main square, from orange juice at breakfast to food stalls after dark.

jemaa_page.name: Jemaa el-Fnaa
jemaa_page.hero_subtitle: Marrakech's great open-air stage, from orange juice at breakfast to smoke, drums and grilled meat after dark.

overview.title: A Square That Changes Shape All Day
overview.p1: Ask ten people what Jemaa el-Fnaa is and you'll get ten answers: a market, a stage, a giant outdoor restaurant, the city's living room. They're all right. The square sits at the edge of the medina and has been where Marrakech gathers since the city was founded in the 11th century, which is why UNESCO recognised its storytelling, music and street traditions as intangible cultural heritage.
overview.p2: Go in the morning and it feels almost sleepy: a few orange juice carts, dried fruit sellers, pigeons, a handful of tourists squinting at maps. Go back at sunset and it is a different place. Storytellers pull circles of listeners around them, Gnawa musicians start up, and dozens of food stalls appear out of nowhere, wrapped in charcoal smoke.
overview.p3: Nobody agrees on where the name comes from. One popular reading is "assembly of the dead", a nod to the days when the square hosted public executions, but you'll hear other versions too. The square doesn't seem to mind the mystery, and neither will you once you're standing in it with a glass of orange juice in your hand.

gallery.subtitle: Swipe through the square from daytime calm to the evening rush.

moods.title: What to Do at Jemaa el-Fnaa, Hour by Hour
moods.subtitle: The square has three very different personalities. Ideally you'll see at least two.

1.title: Quiet, Bright and Easy to Photograph
1.desc: Fresh orange juice from the carts, a slow loop of the square, and a look at the dried fruit and nut stalls. It's the best moment for photos without a crowd in the frame, and a good time to get your bearings before the souks.

2.title: Rooftops, Storytellers and Golden Light
2.desc: Around 4 pm the circles start to form: storytellers, Gnawa musicians, acrobats. Climb to a rooftop café (Café de France and Café Glacier are the classic choices), order a mint tea and watch the square fill up as the light turns gold.

3.title: Smoke, Drums and the Food Stalls
3.desc: The numbered food stalls are up, the grills are hot and the whole square hums. Walk the full circuit before you sit down, then pick a busy stall and eat with a stranger's elbow next to yours. That is the point.

food.title: What to Eat at the Food Stalls
food.p1: Each stall has a number, a row of benches and someone whose job is to convince you to sit down. Don't take the first invitation. Stroll the whole circuit, see what is grilling, and choose the stall with the busiest benches.
food.li1: Grilled merguez sausages and lamb skewers, the safe and delicious starting point.
food.li2: Harira, the thick tomato and lentil soup, ideal on a cool evening.
food.li3: Fried fish and calamari with a squeeze of lemon.
food.li4: Snail soup (babbouche) if you're feeling brave, and sheep's head if you're feeling very brave.
food.li5: Fresh orange juice from the carts and a bag of dates or dried figs for the walk home.
food.p2: Most stalls post a price board. Check it before you order, and confirm what is included with your plate so there are no surprises when the bill arrives. If it's your first evening in Marrakech and you'd rather have someone else do the choosing, a guided food tour is an easy way in.

tips.title: Practical Tips for Visiting Jemaa el-Fnaa

1.title: Getting There
1.desc: Taxis and most walking routes end at the square, so it's an easy landmark to give a driver. Insist on the meter (compteur) in petit taxis. Cars can't enter the medina alleys, so your riad may ask you to meet a porter at the edge.

2.title: Photos and Performers
2.desc: Musicians, henna artists and snake handlers expect a tip if you photograph them, so ask first and agree on an amount. Many travellers skip acts that use chained monkeys or snakes; you'll find plenty to watch without them.

3.title: Staying Comfortable
3.desc: It gets crowded and loud, so wear your bag in front and keep your phone out of back pockets. If someone grabs your hand to start a henna design, just pull away politely and keep walking. Unofficial guides will offer to lead you somewhere; a firm no, thank you is enough.

q1.question: Is Jemaa el-Fnaa free to visit?
q1.answer: Yes. There is no ticket and no gate, the square is open around the clock. Where money does change hands is at the orange juice carts, the food stalls, the rooftop cafés and when you tip a performer.

q2.question: What is the best time to go to Jemaa el-Fnaa?
q2.answer: Late afternoon into the evening. From about 4 pm the storytellers and musicians arrive, and the food stalls start setting up. Come at sunset, stay for dinner. If you just want photos without the crowd, go before 10 am.

q3.question: Is Jemaa el-Fnaa safe at night?
q3.answer: Most visitors have a great time there, and the square is busy until late. Keep your phone and wallet out of easy reach, ignore anyone who grabs your hand to start a henna drawing, and expect a lot of friendly (and slightly pushy) invitations to sit at a stall.

q4.question: How long should I spend at Jemaa el-Fnaa?
q4.answer: Plan on 1.5 to 3 hours. That is enough for a walk around, a juice, a rooftop view and something to eat. If you like people-watching, you will happily stay longer.

q5.question: Is the street food at Jemaa el-Fnaa safe to eat?
q5.answer: Plenty of travellers eat there without a problem. Pick a stall with a queue, choose food that is cooked in front of you, and be careful with raw salads and ice if you have a sensitive stomach. Check the price before you sit down.

seo.og_description: Visiting the Koutoubia Mosque in Marrakech? History, the 77-metre minaret, what non-Muslim visitors can see, the gardens and the best time to go.

koutoubia_page.name: Koutoubia Mosque
koutoubia_page.hero_subtitle: Marrakech's tallest landmark, and the minaret you'll see from almost anywhere.

overview.title: The Landmark You Can Steer By
overview.p1: Built in the 12th century under the Almohad dynasty, the Koutoubia is Marrakech's largest mosque and its most recognisable landmark. Its 77-metre minaret is visible from almost anywhere in the city and served as the model for the Giralda in Seville and the Hassan Tower in Rabat.
overview.p2: The name comes from the Arabic word for 'booksellers', a nod to the manuscript market that once surrounded it. As with all mosques in Morocco, non-Muslim visitors cannot enter the prayer hall, but the gardens around it are lovely and the minaret looks best at sunrise or sunset. It is a five to ten minute walk from Jemaa el-Fnaa.

3.title: Walk to Jemaa el-Fnaa

3.title: Good to Know
3.desc: Non-Muslim visitors cannot enter the mosque, and access is limited to the exterior and gardens. Dress modestly and be respectful around prayer times.

medersa_ben_youssef_page.name: Ben Youssef Madrasa
medersa_ben_youssef_page.hero_subtitle: A former Islamic college where zellige, cedar and carved stucco come together.

overview.title: The Largest Islamic College in North Africa
overview.p1: Ben Youssef Madrasa was founded in the 14th century and rebuilt in 1564–65 under the Saadian dynasty. In its day it housed several hundred students in small cell-like rooms arranged around sunlit courtyards, and the whole place is quiet in a way the nearby souks never are.
overview.p2: The star of the show is the central courtyard: a pool, marble paving and walls covered in zellige, carved stucco and cedar. It is a textbook example of Arab-Andalusian craftsmanship. Recent restoration has brought back much of the original detail, so it's worth a slow look.

palais_bahia_page.name: Bahia Palace
palais_bahia_page.hero_subtitle: Painted ceilings, marble courtyards and orange trees: a palace built to impress.

overview.title: A Palace Built to Impress
overview.p1: Bahia means 'the beautiful', and the name is anything but modest. The palace was built in the late 19th century for the vizier Si Moussa and later expanded by his son Bou Ahmed, who wanted a residence that would outshine everything else in the city.
overview.p2: Inside you'll find the craft of the period at its best: painted cedar ceilings, carved stucco, zellige floors and a big marble courtyard with arcades, one of the most photographed corners of Marrakech. Only part of the complex is open, but it is plenty. Come early, before the tour groups fill the narrow passages.

moods.subtitle: Three details that are easy to walk past.

1.desc: Look up in almost every room. The patterns are hand-painted on cedar and still glow with reds, greens and gold.

2.title: The Marble Courtyard
2.desc: The main courtyard is the showpiece, surrounded by arcades and pleasantly cool even in summer. It is also where crowds gather, so go early.

3.title: Orange and Jasmine Courts
3.desc: Smaller garden courtyards are planted with orange and jasmine trees. They are the quietest corners to sit down and cool off.

tips.title: Practical Tips for Visiting Bahia Palace

1.desc: Walk from Jemaa el-Fnaa in about 20 minutes, or take a petit taxi and ask for the meter. The entrance is on Rue Riad Zitoun el Jdid.

2.title: Timing

3.title: Good to Know
3.desc: There is little signage inside, so a short guide or an audio walk helps. Pair it with El Badi Palace and the Saadian Tombs, both a short walk away.

palais_el_badi_page.name: El Badi Palace
palais_el_badi_page.hero_subtitle: Vast ochre ruins, sunken gardens and storks nesting on the walls.

overview.title: A Palace Meant to Be Incomparable
overview.p1: Sultan Ahmad al-Mansur commissioned El Badi ('The Incomparable') after his victory over the Portuguese in 1578. It was once decorated with gold, marble and cedar wood said to rival the finest palaces of the Islamic world.
overview.p2: Most of that material was stripped away over the following centuries. What remains is a vast open-air ruin of sunken gardens and towering ochre walls, now a favourite nesting site for white storks. Climb the ramparts for views over the medina, and don't miss the carved cedar Koutoubia minbar displayed in the pavilion.

moods.subtitle: Three reasons to climb, walk and look up.

1.title: The Sunken Courtyard
1.desc: A huge central courtyard with pools and sunken gardens gives you a sense of the palace's original scale.

2.title: Ramparts and Storks
2.desc: Walk up to the terraces for views of the medina and the Koutoubia minaret, with storks nesting close by.

3.title: The Koutoubia Minbar
3.desc: A 12th-century carved cedar pulpit is displayed in the pavilion, one of the finest pieces of Almoravid woodwork.

tips.title: Practical Tips for Visiting El Badi Palace

1.desc: El Badi is in the Kasbah district, beside the Saadian Tombs and Bahia Palace. From Jemaa el-Fnaa, take a petit taxi or walk about 25 minutes.

2.title: Timing
2.desc: Open daily, roughly 9:00 to 17:00, with shorter hours during Ramadan. Late afternoon gives golden light on the walls.

3.title: Good to Know
3.desc: Bring a hat and water, because the main courtyard is fully open to the sun. Wear shoes with grip for the ramparts and steps.

q1.question: How long do you need at El Badi Palace?
q1.answer: Plan on 1 to 1.5 hours to walk the courtyard, climb the ramparts and see the minbar.

q2.question: Why are there storks at El Badi Palace?
q2.answer: The high ruined walls make ideal nesting sites for white storks, which is why you'll see nests along the ramparts.

q3.question: How much is the entrance ticket?
q3.answer: Around 70 MAD. Prices and hours can change, so check locally before you go.

q4.question: Is El Badi Palace worth visiting if it's a ruin?

tombeaux_saadiens_page.name: Saadian Tombs

overview.title: A Royal Necropolis Hidden for Centuries
overview.p1: The tombs date back to the 16th-century reign of Sultan Ahmad al-Mansur and hold around 60 members of the Saadian dynasty, plus over a hundred more graves of family members and officials. They were sealed off and forgotten for over two centuries, then rediscovered in 1917 through an aerial survey.
overview.p2: The highlight is the Hall of Twelve Columns, built with Italian Carrara marble and topped with a richly decorated ceiling. The site is small and the entrance passage is narrow, so timing matters more than time: arrive early and you'll enjoy it in peace.

overview.title: The Rif's Favourite Day Out
overview.p1: Akchour sits in the Talassemtane National Park, roughly 45 minutes by road from Chefchaouen. From the village a riverside trail follows the Oued Farda through gorges, past small cafés and swimming pools, to two highlights: the waterfalls and God's Bridge, a natural rock arch high above the valley.
overview.p2: Go prepared. The trail is uneven and there are stretches on rocks, so wear proper shoes, carry water and start early. The pools are cold and lovely in summer. Ask locally about trail conditions, since water levels and access change with the season and after rain. Many visitors hire a local guide.

overview.title: Where the Medina Begins
overview.p1: Bab El Ain is one of the main gateways to the old town, and for many visitors the first taste of Chefchaouen. Step through the arch and the noise of the road fades into narrow lanes lined with small shops, workshops and stalls selling local goods.
overview.p2: Look out for hand-woven wool blankets, local goat cheese, olive products, leather goods and simple pottery. Shopkeepers are used to visitors, so browse freely, compare prices and bargain gently. It's a good morning walk that leads naturally uphill towards Place Outa el Hammam.

overview.title: A Fortress Behind the Main Square
overview.p1: Chefchaouen began as a fortress. The town was founded in 1471 to defend the region, and the Kasbah is the oldest part that still stands, with thick reddish walls and a tower that once looked out for trouble. Today it is calm inside.
overview.p2: Inside you'll find a garden, a few museum spaces and a climb up the tower for views over the blue medina and the Rif. It's small, so pair it with a tea on Place Outa el Hammam and give yourself time for photographs. Hours and access can vary by season, so check locally.

overview.title: The Blue Heart of the Old Town
overview.p1: Al Souika is one of the oldest residential areas in the medina, and where the town's famous blue looks its best. Narrow cobbled lanes wind up and down between blue-washed houses, with carved wooden doors, potted plants and small stairways at every turn.
overview.p2: There's no list of sights to tick off. The pleasure is getting a little lost. Go early, before the day trippers arrive, and keep in mind that these are people's homes. Keep your voice down, ask before photographing anyone and don't block doorways. The reward is a calm, beautiful walk.

overview.title: The Viewpoint Everyone Climbs For
overview.p1: Bouzafar, better known as the Spanish Mosque, was built by the Spanish in the 1920s during the protectorate era and was never used for regular prayer. Its charm is the setting: a whitewashed mosque on a hill with a wide view over Chefchaouen and the mountains behind.
overview.p2: The walk takes roughly 30 to 45 minutes from the medina, mostly uphill on a stony path. Aim to arrive about an hour before sunset, so you can find a spot and watch the light turn the town from white to blue to gold. Bring a light jacket for the descent and a torch or phone light.

overview.title: The Square Where Chefchaouen Meets
overview.p1: Place Outa el Hammam is the main square of the medina and the easiest place to get your bearings. On one side stands the red-walled Kasbah, on the other the Grand Mosque with its unusual octagonal minaret, and in between a row of cafés and restaurants spilling onto the cobbles.
overview.p2: It is a place to sit rather than to tick off. Order a mint tea, watch locals and travellers drift past, and let the light change on the walls. Mornings are calm, evenings are busier, and the square works as the starting point for almost every walk in the medina. Non-Muslim visitors can't enter the mosque, but the exterior is worth a look.

overview.title: Wild Country Behind the Blue Town
overview.p1: Talassemtane National Park was created in 2004 to protect a large area of the Rif Mountains, home to rare Moroccan fir forests, limestone cliffs, streams and small mountain villages. It is one of the greenest, most dramatic landscapes in northern Morocco.
overview.p2: Most visitors come for a day hike, often through Akchour, but longer trekking routes cross the park too. Trails can be steep and poorly marked, and the weather changes fast, so go with a local guide for anything beyond the main routes, and tell someone your plan. Spring and early autumn are the best seasons.

overview.title: The Spring That Made the Town Possible
overview.p1: Ras El Maa, literally 'head of the water', is a natural spring in the hills just outside the east gate of the medina. Cold mountain water rushes down a small stream through the old quarter, and for generations locals have used it for washing clothes and rugs.
overview.p2: It feels more like everyday life than a monument. Watch the stream, sit at a café by the water, or take the path that climbs from here towards the Spanish Mosque. Photograph respectfully: people are going about their day, so ask before you point a camera at someone.
