overview.title: Founded by a Woman in 859
overview.p1: Al Quaraouiyine was founded in 859 by Fatima al-Fihri, a woman from Kairouan who used her inheritance to build a mosque for the neighbourhood. Over the centuries it grew into a major centre of learning, and it is often described as one of the oldest continuously operating educational institutions in the world.
overview.p2: The complex is deep inside the medina and in active use, so non-Muslim visitors can't enter the prayer hall. You can still admire the exterior and the courtyard through the main doors, and take in the surrounding lanes. Access and the library can change, so ask locally, and dress and behave respectfully.

overview.title: The Gate Everyone Photographs
overview.p1: Bab Bou Jeloud is the grand entrance to Fes el-Bali and its most recognisable landmark. The gate was built in the early 20th century and is faced in blue zellige on the outside and green on the inside, colours associated with Fes and with Islam. Its tall arch frames the minaret of the nearby Bou Inania madrasa.
overview.p2: Just inside, two main lanes begin, Talaa Kebira and Talaa Seghira, and the square is lined with cafés and restaurants that are lively all day. Come at dusk for the best photos as the gate lights up, or early in the morning when it is almost empty. It is a handy meeting point before you head into the medina.

bou_inania_madrasa_page.hero_subtitle: A Marinid masterpiece of zellige, carved stucco and cedar on Talaa Kebira.

overview.title: A Religious School Open to Everyone
overview.p1: Bou Inania Madrasa was built in the mid-14th century under the Marinid sultan Abu Inan Faris and is considered one of the finest examples of Marinid architecture. It is one of the few religious buildings in Fes that non-Muslim visitors can enter, which makes it especially worth a stop.
overview.p2: The central courtyard is the highlight: a marble-paved space with a central fountain, walls layered with zellige mosaics, carved stucco and cedar woodwork. Upstairs, small student cells look down on the court. Visit early for a quieter courtyard, and look out for the Dar al-Magana water clock across the lane.

chaouwara_tannery_page.name: Chouara Tannery
chaouwara_tannery_page.hero_subtitle: Stone vats of dye and leather drying on the rooftops, much as it has for centuries.

overview.title: A Medieval Workshop Still at Work
overview.p1: Chouara is the largest and most famous tannery in Fes, and its way of working has changed very little since the Middle Ages. Hides are soaked, scraped and dyed by hand in a honeycomb of round stone vats, then laid out on the rooftops to dry in the sun.
overview.p2: You watch from the terraces of the surrounding leather shops, reached through narrow lanes. Staff will often hand you a sprig of mint to hold to your nose, because the smell is strong. There's no fee for the view, but the shops hope you'll browse, so decide beforehand what you're comfortable with and keep it friendly. Mornings show the vats at their busiest.

overview.title: One of the World's Great Medieval Cities
overview.p1: Fes el-Bali is the old walled heart of Fes, founded more than twelve hundred years ago and listed by UNESCO as a World Heritage Site. It is often described as one of the largest car-free urban areas on earth, a dense web of lanes where donkeys and handcarts still carry goods to souks and workshops.
overview.p2: Getting a little lost is part of the experience, but it helps to have a plan. Start at a main gate such as Bab Bou Jeloud, follow the two main lanes, Talaa Kebira and Talaa Seghira, and pick a few anchors: a madrasa, the tannery, a fountain. Go early, carry cash, save your riad's location offline and consider a licensed guide for the first day.

overview.title: The Best View of the Medina
overview.p1: On the hill north of the old city stand the ruins of tombs linked to the Marinid dynasty, who made Fes an important political and cultural centre in the Middle Ages. Not much remains of the tombs themselves, but the setting is the reason everyone comes.
overview.p2: From the hilltop, the medina unfolds in a panorama of rooftops, minarets and satellite dishes, and the light at sunset turns it gold. The walk up is short but uneven, so wear proper shoes, go with others and come down before it is fully dark. Taxis can also drop you near the top.

overview.title: Another Layer of Fes
overview.p1: The Mellah was established in the 15th century as the Jewish quarter of Fes, next to the royal palace in Fes el-Jdid. For centuries it was a lively neighbourhood of merchants and craftspeople, and it preserves a distinctive chapter of Moroccan Jewish history.
overview.p2: What stands out is the architecture: houses with balconies that face the street, unlike the inward-looking homes of the medina. Walk the main street, then visit the restored Ibn Danan synagogue and the Jewish cemetery, and combine it with the gilded gates of the Royal Palace nearby. Check locally which sites are open and their entry fees.

overview.title: A Caravanserai Turned Woodworking Museum
overview.p1: The Nejjarine Museum of Wooden Arts and Crafts occupies a beautifully restored funduq, an 18th-century inn where merchants once lodged with their animals and goods. The building itself, with its galleries, carved cedar and tiled courtyard, is as much an exhibit as the collection inside.
overview.p2: Inside, tools, furniture, doors and everyday objects explain how Moroccan woodworkers shaped cedar and other woods, which is useful context for everything you see in the medina. Finish on the rooftop café for a view across the rooftops. The carved fountain on Place Nejjarine just outside is also worth a moment.

hassan_ii_page.name: Hassan II Mosque
hassan_ii_page.hero_subtitle: Africa’s largest mosque, rising from the Atlantic with a 210-metre minaret and a prayer hall that holds 25,000 worshippers.

overview.title: Built Over the Ocean
overview.p1: Commissioned by King Hassan II and inaugurated in 1993, this is one of the largest mosques in the world. A third of its surface sits on reclaimed land over the Atlantic, so waves break against the walls at high tide. The minaret rises 210 metres and is visible from much of the city; at night it is lit and can be seen from the Corniche.
overview.p2: Non-Muslims are welcome on guided tours (except during Friday midday prayers). Inside you walk across marble floors under a retractable roof, past carved cedar, zellige and a hammam complex in the basement. The scale is hard to grasp until you stand under the main dome.
overview.p3: Bring modest clothing (shoulders and knees covered); women may be asked to cover their hair. Shoes come off before the prayer hall. Tours last about 45–60 minutes. The exterior esplanade is free and worth a slow walk for photos, especially at sunset.

q1.question: Can non-Muslims visit the Hassan II Mosque?
q1.answer: Yes. Guided tours for non-Muslims are offered several times a day (except Fridays during prayer times). Tickets are sold on site or online; arrive early in high season.

q2.question: What is the best time to visit the Hassan II Mosque?
q2.answer: Morning tours are quieter and cooler. Late afternoon light is beautiful for exterior photos. Avoid Friday midday prayer when tours are limited.

q3.question: Is there a dress code?
q3.answer: Yes. Shoulders and knees should be covered. Women may be asked to cover their hair; scarves are sometimes provided. Shoes are removed before entering the prayer hall.

q4.question: How long does the visit take?
q4.answer: The guided tour lasts about 45–60 minutes. Allow extra time for exterior photos and the esplanade.

q5.question: How much does the ticket cost?
q5.answer: Adult tickets are typically around 130–140 MAD. Prices can change — check the official site or the ticket office on the day.

overview.title: The City’s Living Room by the Sea
overview.p1: The Corniche stretches along Ain Diab and is where Casablancans come to walk, meet friends and watch the ocean. Beach clubs, cafés and seafood restaurants line the route; the Hassan II Mosque sits at the northern end and anchors the skyline.
overview.p2: It is not a wild beach destination — the Atlantic here is often rough — but it is one of the best places in the city for a long walk, a coffee with a view, or a relaxed dinner facing the water.
overview.p3: Come at the end of the day when the light softens and the promenade fills with local families. Combine it easily with a visit to the mosque or a taxi hop to the restaurants further south.

q1.question: Is the Corniche free?
q1.answer: Yes. The promenade is public and free. Beach clubs and restaurants charge for their own services.

q2.question: How long should I spend?
q2.answer: One to two hours is enough for a good walk and a café stop; longer if you stay for dinner.

q3.question: Is it safe at night?
q3.answer: The main stretch is well frequented in the evening. Use normal city awareness, especially in quieter side streets.

q4.question: Can I swim?
q4.answer: Conditions vary and the sea can be rough. Check locally and prefer organised beach club areas if you want to enter the water.

q5.question: How do I combine it with the mosque?
q5.answer: The Hassan II Mosque sits at the northern end of the Corniche — easy to visit both in the same half-day.

seo.title: Quartier Habous, Casablanca: Neo-Moorish Souks & Royal Palace Area | MoroccoTripMap
seo.description: Explore Quartier Habous in Casablanca: 1930s neo-Moorish architecture, craft souks, cafés and the area around the Royal Palace.
seo.og_description: A 1930s neo-Moorish neighbourhood of arcades, craft shops and quiet cafés near the Royal Palace.

habous_page.name: Quartier Habous
habous_page.hero_subtitle: A 1930s neo-Moorish neighbourhood of arcades, craft shops and quiet cafés near the Royal Palace.

overview.title: Casablanca’s Planned Medina
overview.p1: Built in the 1930s under the French Protectorate, the Quartier Habous (also called the Nouvelle Médina) was designed as a modern interpretation of a traditional medina. Arcaded streets, whitewashed walls and green-tiled roofs give it a calm, ordered feel that contrasts with the denser Old Medina.
overview.p2: It is a good place to browse crafts, leather and traditional clothing without the intensity of larger tourist souks. The Mahkama du Pacha and the nearby Royal Palace walls are part of the same ensemble.
overview.p3: Cafés in the main squares are ideal for mint tea. The area works well as a half-day stop between downtown and a taxi to the Corniche or the Old Medina.

2.desc: Leather, textiles and traditional goods in a less intense setting than big tourist markets.

3.title: Royal Palace Area
3.desc: Walls of the Royal Palace and the Mahkama du Pacha nearby.

tips.title: Practical Tips for Visiting Quartier Habous

1.title: Getting there
1.desc: Taxi from the centre or Corniche. Drivers know ‘Habous’ or ‘Nouvelle Médina’.

2.title: Timing
2.desc: Morning for quieter streets; late afternoon for softer light and café atmosphere.

3.title: Shopping
3.desc: Prices are often calmer than in major tourist souks, but friendly bargaining is still normal for crafts.

q1.question: Is Quartier Habous free to visit?
q1.answer: Yes. The streets and squares are public. Individual shops and cafés set their own prices.

q2.question: How long should I spend?
q2.answer: One to two hours is enough for a walk, a few shops and a tea stop.

q3.question: Is it the same as the Old Medina?
q3.answer: No. Habous is a 1930s planned district (Nouvelle Médina). The Old Medina is the older, denser core near the port.

q4.question: Can I see the Royal Palace?
q4.answer: The palace itself is not open to the public, but you can walk along the exterior walls in the same area.

q5.question: Is it good for shopping?
q5.answer: Yes for crafts and traditional items in a calmer setting than Marrakech or Fez souks.

seo.description: Visit Casablanca’s Old Medina: compact streets, food stalls, everyday life and how it compares to Marrakech or Fez.
seo.og_description: A compact, working medina of food stalls, spice shops and everyday Casablanca life.

old_medina_page.name: Old Medina
old_medina_page.hero_subtitle: A compact, working medina of food stalls, spice shops and everyday Casablanca life — quieter than Marrakech or Fez.

overview.title: Small, Authentic, Still Lived-In
overview.p1: Casablanca’s Old Medina is much smaller than those of Marrakech or Fez. It is a dense tangle of lanes where residents shop for vegetables, spices and household goods. Tourist-oriented stalls exist, but the overall atmosphere is local rather than staged.
overview.p2: It sits close to the port and the city centre, so it is easy to combine with Rick’s Café, the Marché Central or a walk toward the Corniche. Keep an eye on your belongings as you would in any busy urban market.
overview.p3: Do not expect the architectural drama of imperial medinas. Come for a slice of ordinary Casablanca life, a cheap snack and a sense of the city’s older layers before the Art Deco boom.

seo.title: Place Mohammed V, Casablanca: Art Deco & Civic Architecture | MoroccoTripMap
seo.description: Discover Place Mohammed V in Casablanca: the civic square framed by Art Deco and neo-Mauresque public buildings.
seo.og_description: The civic heart of Casablanca, framed by imposing Art Deco and neo-Mauresque public buildings.

place_mv_page.name: Place Mohammed V
place_mv_page.hero_subtitle: The civic heart of Casablanca, framed by imposing Art Deco and neo-Mauresque public buildings.

overview.title: Downtown’s Architectural Showcase
overview.p1: Place Mohammed V is the ceremonial and administrative core of central Casablanca. Around it stand the wilaya (prefecture), the law courts, the post office and other public buildings that mix Art Deco lines with neo-Mauresque detail — a signature of the Protectorate-era city plan.
overview.p2: It is not a place you linger for hours, but it is essential if you care about 20th-century architecture. The square and its fountains work well as a starting point for a walking tour of the downtown grid.
overview.p3: Combine it with the nearby Villa des Arts, the Marché Central or a tram ride toward the Corniche. Early morning or late afternoon light is best for photographs of the façades.

seo.title: Rick’s Café Casablanca: The Famous Film Bar, Menu & How to Visit | MoroccoTripMap
seo.description: Visit Rick’s Café in Casablanca: a recreation of the 1942 film bar, with piano, period décor, reservations and practical tips.
seo.og_description: A loving recreation of the bar from the 1942 film, with piano, period décor and a refined menu.

ricks_page.name: Rick’s Café
ricks_page.hero_subtitle: A loving recreation of the bar from the 1942 film, complete with piano, period décor and a refined menu.

overview.title: Of All the Cafés in All the World
overview.p1: There was no real Rick’s Café in the 1942 film — the set was built in Hollywood. Decades later, a former American diplomat opened this restaurant in Casablanca as a careful homage: arched interiors, warm lighting, a grand piano and a menu that mixes international and Moroccan dishes.
overview.p2: It is popular with visitors and locals for special occasions. Reservations are strongly recommended, especially for dinner and weekends. Dress is smart-casual.
overview.p3: Even if you do not eat here, the building and the story make it a stop on many city tours. It sits close to the Old Medina and is an easy taxi ride from the centre or the Corniche.

overview.p2: The building itself is part of the attraction: clean lines, period details and a scale that feels intimate rather than institutional. Check current exhibitions before you go, as the programme changes regularly.
overview.p3: It pairs well with a walk through the surrounding neighbourhood or a visit to other downtown landmarks such as Place Mohammed V. Allow about an hour, more if a particular show draws you in.

seo.title: Essaouira Travel Guide 2026 | Medina, Ramparts, Beach & Riads | MoroccoTripMap
seo.description: Plan your trip to Essaouira: medina and ramparts, Atlantic beach, port, best riads and hotels, seafood, Gnaoua culture, a 3-day itinerary, day trips, and practical tips.
seo.og_description: Medina, ramparts, beach, riads, seafood and a ready-made itinerary for Essaouira, all in one guide.

essaouira_page.hero_subtitle: Atlantic wind, a blue-and-white UNESCO medina, ramparts over the ocean and some of Morocco’s best day-caught seafood — Essaouira is the relaxed, salty contrast to Marrakech.

overview.title: Welcome to the Windy City of the Atlantic
overview.p1: Essaouira is the Atlantic answer to Morocco’s imperial cities — a place where the wind does half the storytelling. Whitewashed lanes lean into blue shutters, Portuguese-era cannons still face the open ocean, and the morning catch is grilled a few metres from the boats that brought it in. UNESCO listed the medina for good reason: it was planned in the 18th century with straighter lines and sea air, so you can wander without the deep-maze intensity of Fès or Marrakech.
overview.p2: Come for the seafood at the port stalls, stay for the Gnaoua rhythms that still pulse through summer nights, and leave with salt on your skin and thuya resin on your hands. Two or three nights are enough to walk both Skalas, lose an afternoon in the workshops, and watch the islands turn black against a pink horizon. Pair it with Marrakech if you want contrast; come alone if you want the wind to slow you down.

mellah.desc: Historic Jewish quarter, synagogue and a quieter corner of the medina’s layered past.

bargain.desc: Thuya and silver are local specialties. Bargain politely; prices are usually softer than Marrakech.

water.desc: Currents and wind can be strong. Swim where locals do and follow flag advice if posted.

q1.question: How many days do I need in Essaouira?
q1.answer: Two full days cover the medina, port, Skala and beach. Three days allow a slower pace or a trip to Sidi Kaouki.

q2.question: Is Essaouira windy all year?
q2.answer: Yes, the trade wind is part of the climate. Spring and autumn are pleasant; summer is warm but rarely as hot as inland cities.

q3.question: Is the medina safe to walk at night?
q3.answer: The main areas and Place Moulay Hassan stay lively. Use normal city awareness in quieter lanes late at night.

q4.question: Can I visit the Île de Mogador?
q4.answer: Landing is usually restricted (nature reserve). Most visitors enjoy the islands as a view from the beach and ramparts.

detailed_itinerary.day1_m: Morning — Skala de la Ville & ramparts
detailed_itinerary.day1_md: Start on the western sea walls while the light is soft. Walk the full Skala de la Ville: brass cannons, Atlantic spray and the first clear view of the Mogador islands. The alizé is strongest here — lean into it.
detailed_itinerary.day1_ad: Drop into the white-and-blue grid. Watch marquetry in open workshops, compare silver and argan quality, and pause on Place Moulay Hassan for juice. The medina is compact — you can cover a lot without rushing.
detailed_itinerary.day1_ed: Head to the harbour as the boats settle. Point to fresh sardines or bream, agree the price, and eat with your hands while seagulls argue overhead. Finish with mint tea back toward the square.
detailed_itinerary.day2_m: Morning — Beach arc or Skala du Port
detailed_itinerary.day2_md: Walk south along the wide sandy bay, or climb the port-side Skala for cannons above the blue fleet. Kitesurf schools set up early when the wind is clean; even a long barefoot walk is worth the salt air.
detailed_itinerary.day2_ad: Explore the quieter Mellah lanes, then circle back through galleries and craft streets you skipped yesterday. Essaouira rewards the second pass — details appear when you stop hunting for “the” photo.
detailed_itinerary.day2_e: Evening — Gnaoua or a courtyard table
detailed_itinerary.day2_ed: If a performance or festival set is on, go. Otherwise book a medina courtyard or rooftop out of the wind — evenings cool fast even in summer. Ask your riad what is playing that night.
detailed_itinerary.day3_m: Morning — Last rampart light or beach camels
detailed_itinerary.day3_md: Optional short camel ride on the beach (agree price and duration first), or a final unhurried walk on the Skala with fewer tour groups. Coffee on Place Moulay Hassan is a good goodbye ritual.
detailed_itinerary.day3_a: Afternoon — Toward Marrakech or the coast
detailed_itinerary.day3_ad: Many travellers continue to Marrakech (about 2.5–3 hours by road) or south toward Agadir and Taghazout. If you stay a fourth night, use it for pure beach time or a longer workshop visit.
detailed_itinerary.day3_ed: One more rooftop mint tea if you overnight, or an evening departure depending on bus and transfer times. Keep a layer handy — the wind does not care about your schedule.

overview.title: Where the Catch Comes In
overview.p1: Essaouira’s port is still a working fishing harbour. Blue wooden boats crowd the quays, nets dry in the wind, and seagulls dive for scraps. This is not a staged attraction — the catch lands here every morning and the grills fire up soon after.
overview.p2: Climb the Skala platform above the harbour for cannons, stone walls and a full view of the fleet. Then drop back to the stalls: point to a fish, agree the price, and watch it hit the plancha.
overview.p3: Combine the port with Place Moulay Hassan and a short medina loop in the same half-day. Bring a light jacket — the alizé rarely rests.

agadir_page.hero_subtitle: Wide Atlantic bay, modern corniche, hilltop Kasbah views and a gateway to Taghazout surf and Paradise Valley — Agadir is Morocco’s easy beach capital.

overview.title: Welcome to Morocco’s Atlantic Beach Capital
overview.p1: Agadir is Morocco’s big Atlantic beach city — rebuilt after the 1960 earthquake into a wide, modern resort rather than a medina maze. What you get instead is a long sandy bay, a palm-lined corniche, and a hilltop Kasbah that still watches over everything. The pace is slower than Marrakech, sunnier than the north, and built for days that end with salt on your skin and grilled fish on the plate.
overview.p2: Climb the Kasbah at golden hour for the classic curve of the bay. Lose a morning in Souk El Had, one of the largest markets in the country. Use the city as a base for Taghazout’s surf breaks, Paradise Valley’s palm pools, and day trips into the Anti-Atlas. Three to five nights work well if you want beach time without giving up day-trip options.

1.title: Sun protection
1.desc: Agadir is sunny most of the year. Use high SPF, a hat and drink water on the beach and at the Kasbah.

2.title: Stay near the beach
2.desc: Most visitors want easy sand access. Corniche and beach hotels maximise convenience.

3.title: Kasbah by taxi or walk

transport.title: Getting there
transport.desc: Agadir Al Massira Airport (AGA) is the main gateway. Taxis and hotel transfers cover the city; grand taxis for Taghazout.

bargain.title: Souk shopping

water.desc: Atlantic water is cooler than the Med. Respect flags and local advice on currents.

q1.question: How many days in Agadir?
q1.answer: Three days cover beach, Kasbah and souk. Five days allow Taghazout or Paradise Valley without rushing.

q2.question: Is Agadir only a beach resort?
q2.answer: Mainly yes — the city is modern after 1960. Culture comes from day trips, the souk and the Kasbah viewpoint.

q3.question: Is the beach safe for swimming?
q3.answer: Main sections are popular and often supervised in season. Always follow flags and local advice.

q4.question: Can I visit Taghazout as a day trip?
q4.answer: Yes. Grand taxis and tours run frequently; many visitors go for the day and return to Agadir hotels.

overview.p1: Agadir Beach is the reason most visitors come: a broad, long arc of sand that can feel almost endless at low season. The water is Atlantic-cool, the backdrop is modern hotels and palms, and the mood is resort rather than wild coast.
overview.p2: Walk it at sunrise before the loungers fill, or at sunset when the Kasbah ridge catches the last light. Sections in front of big hotels are busier; walk further for more space.
overview.p3: Pair the beach with a Kasbah viewpoint the same day and a port or corniche dinner. The beach alone can fill hours; it does not need a complicated plan.

overview.title: Above the Bay
overview.p1: The Kasbah (Agadir Oufella) sits on the hill north of the modern city. The 1960 earthquake left little of the old fortress standing, but the viewpoint remains the single best place to understand the curve of the bay, the port and the long hotel strip.
overview.p2: Come for the panorama, not for elaborate ruins. Golden hour and clear mornings are ideal; midday haze can flatten the view. A short taxi ride saves the steep walk in the heat.
overview.p3: Combine with the beach or corniche the same day. The visit itself is short — thirty to sixty minutes for most people.

overview.title: One of Morocco’s Largest Markets
overview.p1: Souk El Had is not a polished tourist bazaar — it is a working market where Agadir shops for food, clothes and household goods. The scale surprises first-time visitors: aisles of olives, spices, butchers, fabrics and small electronics under covered halls.
overview.p2: Go with patience and a sense of humour. Taste when invited, compare prices, and keep phones and wallets secure in denser sections. Mornings are livelier for produce; afternoons work for browsing.
overview.p3: A guided food walk can help if you want context; otherwise one or two hours of wandering is enough for most travellers.

overview.title: The City’s Seafront Living Room

overview.p2: Use it to move between beach sections, to find a café, or simply to walk off dinner. Evenings are the busiest and the most social.
overview.p3: Pair with a Kasbah viewpoint earlier in the day and a port grill if you want fish with more character than hotel menus.

overview.title: Surf Village North of Agadir
overview.p1: Taghazout is the surf village that sits just north of Agadir’s resort sprawl. The vibe shifts: fewer high-rises, more boards on rooftops, cafés that open to the sound of the Atlantic. Reef breaks attract surfers year-round; non-surfers still come for the village scale and coastal walks.
overview.p2: A half-day is enough for lunch and a look; a full day works if you take a lesson or simply sit with the ocean. Agree taxi fares before leaving Agadir, or book a transfer.
overview.p3: It is an easy add-on to an Agadir base and a calmer contrast to the main bay’s hotel strip.

overview.title: Welcome to Morocco’s Northern Gateway
overview.p1: Tangier is where Africa and Europe almost touch — Atlantic on one side, Mediterranean on the other, and Spain often visible across the strait. The medina still feels layered: Kasbah walls, steep lanes, and the old international-zone stories that writers never quite stopped telling. Below, the modern city stretches along the bay with cafés, beaches and a ferry terminal that keeps the place looking outward.
overview.p2: Climb the Kasbah for the classic view over the port and the strait. Lose an afternoon in the medina around the Petit Socco, drink mint tea at Café Hafa with the sea below, and leave time for Cap Spartel and the Caves of Hercules when you want the coast without the city noise. Two to four nights work well if Tangier is a gateway in or out of Morocco.

tanger_kasbah_page.name: Tangier Kasbah
tanger_kasbah_page.hero_subtitle: Ramparts, museum and the classic view over Tangier bay.

overview.title: Above the Port and the Strait
overview.p1: The Kasbah sits on the highest point of the old city, looking out over the port and the Strait of Gibraltar. On a clear day Spain is a pale line on the water. The walls and the museum matter, but the real reason most people climb up is that view — and the quieter lanes once you leave the main gate behind.
overview.p2: Give yourself time to walk the ramparts slowly. The Kasbah Museum (in the former Dar el-Makhzen) is worth an hour if you like objects and context; if not, the terraces alone justify the walk.
overview.p3: Come in the morning for softer light, or late afternoon when the bay starts to glow. Combine with the medina below rather than treating it as a separate outing.

q1.answer: The outdoor areas are largely free to walk; the museum has a ticket — check the current price at the door.

q2.question: How long do I need?
q2.answer: 45 to 90 minutes for most visits; longer if you stay in the museum.

q3.question: Is the walk steep?
q3.answer: Yes from the lower medina — wear comfortable shoes and take it slowly in the heat.

q4.question: Do I need a guide at Tangier Kasbah?
q4.answer: Optional for a simple visit; useful for historical context.

q5.question: Is Tangier Kasbah suitable for families?

tanger_medina_page.name: Tangier Medina
tanger_medina_page.hero_subtitle: Petit Socco, Kasbah approaches and the layered streets of the old town.

overview.title: Steep Lanes and the Old International Air
overview.p1: Tangier’s medina is not as vast as Fes or as theatrical as Marrakech’s. It is steeper, tighter, and still marked by the decades when the city was an international zone. You feel that in the mix of languages on shop signs and in the way the lanes drop toward the port.
overview.p2: Start from the Grand Socco, slip toward the Petit Socco, and let the slope decide your route. The American Legation sits on one edge; the Kasbah crowns the top. Between them, ordinary life continues — groceries, workshops, kids on steps.
overview.p3: A half-day is enough for a first pass. Stay longer if you like getting lost on purpose.

overview.title: Where Two Seas Meet
overview.p1: Cap Spartel is the northwest tip of Africa that travellers come to for a simple idea: standing where the Atlantic and the Mediterranean meet. The lighthouse, the wind and the wide view matter more than any single monument.
overview.p2: It is a short drive from Tangier. Go early if you can — coaches arrive later, and the light is cleaner in the morning. Pair it with the Caves of Hercules on the same half-day; they sit close enough that splitting them into two trips wastes time.
overview.p3: Dress for wind. Even on warm days the point can feel sharp.

overview.title: Sea Grotto and the Africa Window
overview.p1: The Caves of Hercules sit on the coast west of Tangier, famous for the opening that looks — with a little goodwill — like the map of Africa. Myth and geology share the same postcard. The visit is short; the setting is the point.
overview.p2: You walk down into the grotto, watch the sea light through the aperture, and step back out into the wind. It is popular, so the magic is stronger early or late. Combining with Cap Spartel is the sensible plan.
overview.p3: Watch your step on wet stone and keep an eye on children near the edges.

tanger_hafa_page.name: Café Hafa
tanger_hafa_page.hero_subtitle: Terraces stacked above the strait — Tangier’s most famous café pause.

overview.title: Mint Tea on the Cliff
overview.p1: Café Hafa is less about the coffee than about the seat. Terraces step down the cliff, mint tea arrives in glasses, and the Strait of Gibraltar does the rest. Writers and musicians made it famous; locals still use it as a place to sit and watch the light change.
overview.p2: You do not need a long stay. An hour with a tea is enough. Come for late afternoon if you want the softer colours; mornings are quieter if you dislike crowds.
overview.p3: It is a café with a view, not a full restaurant experience — keep expectations there and you will leave happy.

overview.title: The City’s Everyday Crossroads
overview.p1: The Grand Socco is not a monument you photograph for an hour. It is the square where Tangier changes gear: taxis, buses, shoppers, and the arch that leads into the medina. Place du 9 Avril is its official name; everyone still says Grand Socco.
overview.p2: Use it as a landmark. Meet friends here, start a medina walk from here, catch a taxi from here. The cinema façade and the surrounding cafés give it a face, but the energy is the crowd itself.
overview.p3: Ten to thirty minutes is enough unless you sit down for a coffee and watch the flow.

tanger_legation_page.name: American Legation

overview.title: A Quiet Museum in the Medina
overview.p1: The American Legation is easy to miss if you only chase viewpoints. Tucked into the medina, it is the first American public property abroad and now a museum of art, maps and Tangier’s international century. It rewards people who like rooms with stories more than rooftop selfies.
overview.p2: Check opening hours before you go — they are not the same as a souk stall. The visit is compact: galleries, a courtyard, and enough context to understand why Tangier mattered to so many outsiders.
overview.p3: Pair it with a medina walk so you are not making a special trip across town for a single small museum.

overview.title: Bay Sand Below the City
overview.p1: Tangier Beach is the straightforward sandy strip along the bay. It will not compete with Agadir for resort polish, and it is not a wild Atlantic surf beach. It is where you go when the medina slopes have been enough and you want the horizon without a drive to Cap Spartel.
overview.p2: Weekends draw local families. Weekday mornings are calmer. The corniche above gives you cafés and a place to sit when the wind picks up.
overview.p3: Swim only where it looks supervised and sensible; currents and water quality can vary — follow local practice.

ouarzazate_page.hero_subtitle: Gateway to the desert — kasbahs, film studios, Aït Benhaddou and the road south.

overview.title: Welcome to the Door of the Desert
overview.p1: Ouarzazate sits where the High Atlas drops toward the desert — a practical town of wide avenues, film studios and old kasbahs rather than a deep medina maze. People stop here for Aït Benhaddou, the palm sea of Skoura, and as a launch point for the Draa Valley or longer desert runs toward Zagora and Merzouga. The light is what the studios came for: hard, clear, and good for both cinema and late-afternoon walks.
overview.p2: In town, Kasbah Taourirt is the landmark you can walk to. A short drive takes you to Aït Benhaddou, Tifoultoute, Fint oasis or the studios if you care about sets. Two nights work if Ouarzazate is a bridge; three if you want Skoura and a slower pace without racing the desert transfer.

q1.answer: Two full days cover Taourirt, a studio and Aït Benhaddou. Three allow Skoura or Fint without rushing.

ouarzazate_taourirt_page.name: Kasbah Taourirt
ouarzazate_taourirt_page.hero_subtitle: Mud-brick lanes and rooftop views you can walk to from the centre.

overview.title: The Kasbah at the Heart of Town
overview.p1: Kasbah Taourirt sits right in Ouarzazate, not half an hour down a tourist road. It was a Glaoui stronghold; today the restored sections and the maze of crumbling courtyards give you the texture of a desert-edge kasbah without leaving town. Climb for the rooftop views over the modern avenues and the hills beyond.
overview.p2: Go in the morning while the alleys still hold shade. Some rooms are restored with exhibits; others are open shells. Wear closed shoes — mud brick and uneven steps are the rule.
overview.p3: An hour or two is enough for most visits. Pair it with a café in town rather than treating it as a full-day outing.

q3.answer: Some stair sections — take your time on worn steps.

ouarzazate_studios_page.name: Atlas Studios
ouarzazate_studios_page.hero_subtitle: Outdoor stages and Egyptian gates — the “Hollywood of the desert” for the curious.

overview.title: Film Sets at the Edge of the Desert
overview.p1: Atlas Studios is the large outdoor complex on the edge of Ouarzazate where crews have built Egyptian temples, fortified walls and desert towns for decades of film and TV. You visit on a guided tour of the standing sets — it is less a museum than a walk through painted plaster and plywood under hard desert light.
overview.p2: If you love cinema logistics, you will enjoy the scale. If you only want kasbahs and palms, one studio visit is enough — or skip it for Aït Benhaddou and Skoura.
overview.p3: Tours run on a schedule; check times when you arrive. Closed shoes help on dusty ground between sets.

moods.subtitle: Three ways to experience Atlas Studios

q1.answer: Visits are organised as guided tours of the sets — turn up for the next departure.

q2.answer: Typically 40 to 90 minutes depending on the group and the route.

q3.question: Is it worth it if I am not a film fan?
q3.answer: Optional — prioritise Aït Benhaddou if time is short.

ouarzazate_ait_page.name: Aït Benhaddou
ouarzazate_ait_page.hero_subtitle: UNESCO mud-brick village — the silhouette everyone knows from film and postcards.

overview.title: The Classic Ksar on the Old Caravan Road
overview.p1: Aït Benhaddou is the ksar that defined the postcard of southern Morocco for many travellers: a cluster of earthen buildings climbing a hillside above a seasonal river, about thirty minutes from Ouarzazate. It is a living village as well as a UNESCO site, which means you share the lanes with residents, guides and tour groups.
overview.p2: Cross the riverbed (or the bridge when the water is up), climb toward the granary at the top, and give yourself time on the way down. The view back over the valley is the reason the climb is worth the heat.
overview.p3: Early morning is the difference between a calm visit and a crowded one. Midday on the open mud slopes is harsh from late spring onward.

moods.subtitle: Three ways to experience Aït Benhaddou

1.title: Hillside lanes
1.desc: The slow rise to the top granary.

2.title: Postcard ksar
2.desc: Why this village appears in so many films.

3.title: View from above
3.desc: Palm and dry river from the highest roofs.

q1.question: How far from Ouarzazate?
q1.answer: About 30 minutes by car.

q2.question: Is there an entry fee?
q2.answer: A community fee is usual at the entrance — small notes help.

q3.question: Can I stay overnight?
q3.answer: A few simple guesthouses exist; most visitors day-trip from Ouarzazate.

q4.question: Do I need a guide at Aït Benhaddou?
q4.answer: Optional for a simple visit; useful for history and safe paths on fragile mud brick.

q5.question: Is Aït Benhaddou suitable for families?
q5.answer: Yes with supervision on steps, rooftops and uneven ground.

food.title: Simple meals near the ksar
food.p1: Cafés and tagine spots sit on the modern side of the river. Inside the ksar, expect little beyond tea if anything.
food.p2: Eat where other travellers and locals are sitting — turnover matters in the heat.
food.li1: Tagine with a view on the new side
food.li4: Avoid undercooked salads if your stomach is sensitive
food.li5: Lunch back in town if you prefer more choice

tips.title: Practical Tips for Visiting Aït Benhaddou

1.desc: Coach groups peak mid-morning to early afternoon. Before 9–10 am the lanes are quieter and the mud is cooler underfoot.

2.title: River crossing
2.desc: In dry months you walk the riverbed; after rain use the bridge. Shoes you do not mind getting dusty are essential.

3.title: Guides
3.desc: Official guides wait at the entrance. Useful for history; not required if you only want the climb and the view. Agree the price before you start.

ouarzazate_tifoultoute_page.name: Kasbah Tifoultoute

overview.title: Kasbah Above the Plain
overview.p1: Tifoultoute sits on a rise a short drive from Ouarzazate, a kasbah that has seen better centuries but still holds a strong outline against the sky. It is less visited than Aït Benhaddou, which means more space to walk and fewer sales pitches on the path.
overview.p2: You come for the position and the light, not for a fully restored interior. Some rooms may be closed or fragile — stay on sound footing and treat it as a viewpoint with history attached.
overview.p3: Late afternoon suits the walls; midday is harsh and less photogenic.

overview.title: Props, Posters and the Local Film Story
overview.p1: The Cinema Museum gathers costumes, posters, models and the story of how this desert town became a base for international shoots. It is compact, shaded and useful if you want context without committing to a full Atlas Studios tour.
overview.p2: Families and film fans get the most from it. If your trip is only about ksars and palms, you can skip it without regret.
overview.p3: Check opening hours — they are not the same as a kasbah you can walk into at dawn.

overview.title: Green Break in the Rocky Landscape
overview.p1: Fint is a small oasis pocket in the rocky country south of Ouarzazate: palms, a thread of water, and a slower rhythm than the ksar circuit. You come for the green and the quiet, not for a list of monuments.
overview.p2: A local driver helps if you want tracks that are not obvious from the main road. The visit is short — an hour or two of walking and sitting is enough.
overview.p3: Bring more water than the short distance suggests; the surrounding rock throws heat back at you.

ouarzazate_skoura_page.name: Skoura
ouarzazate_skoura_page.hero_subtitle: Palm grove, scattered ksars and tracks between the trees — best with a local driver.

overview.title: A Sea of Palms East of Town
overview.p1: Skoura is less a single monument than a wide palm oasis east of Ouarzazate. Ksars rise among the trees; tracks weave between gardens and dry walls. The pleasure is the density of green after the bare plains, and the slower tempo once you leave the main road.
overview.p2: A half-day with a driver who knows the grove is worth more than a rushed photo stop at the first kasbah you see. Amridil is the name you will hear most for a visit inside a historic house.
overview.p3: Midday in summer is heavy under the palms too — morning or late afternoon is more comfortable.

overview.title: Water on the Desert Edge
overview.p1: Lake Mansour Eddahbi is the reservoir that holds water for the region and offers Ouarzazate a different horizon: open water, birds in season, and shoreline walks instead of kasbah stairs. It is not a swimming resort; it is a landscape stop when you need a break from earthen walls.
overview.p2: A short visit works at the end of a town day or before a longer transfer. Bring binoculars if you care about birds; bring a wind layer if the afternoon breeze picks up.
overview.p3: Access points vary — a driver who knows a quiet shore is more useful than a random pull-off.

rabat_page.hero_subtitle: Morocco’s capital of calm power: Kasbah of the Udayas, Hassan Tower, Mohammed V Mausoleum, Chellah ruins and Atlantic light — Rabat rewards slower walks than the imperial inland cities.

overview.title: Why Visit Rabat?
overview.p1: Rabat combines political capital, Atlantic coastline and layered history: Almohad walls, Andalusian gardens in the Kasbah of the Udayas, the unfinished Hassan Tower, the royal mausoleum and the Roman–medieval site of Chellah. It feels more ordered and greener than Marrakech or Fez.
overview.p2: Two to three days cover the Kasbah, Hassan complex, Chellah and the medina without rushing. Use Rabat as a calm base between Tangier and Casablanca or before heading inland.

q1.question: How many days in Rabat?
q1.answer: Two full days cover Kasbah, Hassan complex and Chellah. Three allow the marina, museum or a short day trip.

q2.question: Is Rabat worth visiting vs Casablanca?
q2.answer: Yes if you want monuments, a calmer capital and Atlantic walks. Casablanca is more business and modern scale.

q3.question: Can I visit the Hassan Tower interior?
q3.answer: The tower exterior and esplanade are the visit; access to the interior is generally not for the public.

q4.question: Is the Kasbah free?
q4.answer: Walking the lanes is free; the museum and some spaces may charge. Gardens are part of the Kasbah visit.

rabat_oudayas_page.name: Kasbah of the Udayas
rabat_oudayas_page.hero_subtitle: Blue-and-white lanes above the Bouregreg — the postcard corner of the capital.

overview.title: Where the river meets the Atlantic walls
overview.p1: The Kasbah of the Udayas sits on the bluff where the Bouregreg meets the ocean. Whitewashed walls, blue doors and narrow lanes give Rabat its most photogenic face — and a living neighbourhood, not a empty set.
overview.p2: Enter through the monumental Almohad gate, wander toward the platform overlooking Salé and the river mouth, then drop into the Andalusian Garden if you want shade. The kasbah rewards slow walking more than a checklist dash.
overview.p3: Come early for soft light on the blue paint, or late afternoon when the river breeze picks up and day-trip coaches have left. Pair it with the nearby medina or a tram ride back toward the ville nouvelle.

q1.question: Is there an entry fee for the kasbah?
q1.answer: The residential kasbah streets are free to walk. The Andalusian Garden and museum areas may have separate modest tickets.

q2.question: How long should I spend here?
q2.answer: One to two hours covers the gate, main lanes and viewpoint without rushing.

q3.question: Is it suitable with children?
q3.answer: Yes — watch steps near the viewpoint and keep little ones close on narrow lanes when scooters pass.

q4.question: Best time of day?
q4.answer: Morning for quieter streets and softer light; late afternoon for breeze and warmer wall colours.

q5.question: Can I combine it with Chellah the same day?
q5.answer: Yes. Do the kasbah in the morning, then taxi or drive to Chellah in the afternoon when you want more space.

food.title: Tea with a view, lunch in the medina
food.p1: Cafés inside and just outside the kasbah serve tea and simple snacks with river views. For a fuller meal, walk toward the medina restaurants a few minutes away.
food.p2: This is a neighbourhood first — expect terrace tea more than fine dining inside the walls.

tips.title: Practical Tips for Visiting the Kasbah of the Udayas

1.title: Start at the gate, finish at the platform
1.desc: Enter by the main Almohad gate, loop the residential lanes without forcing every dead-end, and save the river viewpoint for last when the light is best. Wear comfortable shoes — cobbles and short climbs are constant.

2.title: Respect that people live here
2.desc: Doors open onto family homes. Keep voices down at prayer times, ask before photographing residents, and skip drones. The blue paint is charming; the privacy of the street is not a backdrop for loud groups.

3.title: Link it on foot with the medina and gardens
3.desc: From the kasbah you can walk into Rabat’s medina in minutes. The Andalusian Garden sits beside the kasbah for shade. Tram and taxis connect easily if you continue to Hassan Tower or the ville nouvelle afterward.

rabat_hassan_page.name: Hassan Tower
rabat_hassan_page.hero_subtitle: The unfinished minaret that still defines Rabat’s skyline.

overview.title: An Almohad ambition left open to the sky
overview.p1: Hassan Tower was meant to anchor one of the largest mosques of the Almohad age. The minaret rose; the prayer hall columns never fully became a finished mosque. What remains is one of Morocco’s most recognisable silhouettes.
overview.p2: You walk the esplanade among the column stumps, look up at the tower’s carved faces, and understand the scale the builders intended. The site is open, windy and inseparable from the neighbouring Mohammed V Mausoleum.
overview.p3: Visit in the morning if you want softer light on the stone, or late day when the tower catches warmer colour. Guard changing and formal visits nearby can draw crowds — check the rhythm of the mausoleum if you plan both.

moods.subtitle: Three ways to experience the tower and esplanade

q1.question: Can I climb Hassan Tower?
q1.answer: No. The minaret is not open for climbing; you experience it from the esplanade.

q2.question: Is there a ticket?
q2.answer: The esplanade is generally free to walk; the mausoleum next door follows its own entry rules and dress expectations.

q3.question: How much time do I need?
q3.answer: Thirty to sixty minutes for the tower and columns; add time if you enter the mausoleum.

q4.question: Is it far from the kasbah?
q4.answer: A short taxi or a longer walk — many visitors do kasbah in the morning and Hassan Tower after lunch.

q5.question: Best photos?
q5.answer: Morning side light or late afternoon colour on the stone; midday is harsher and busier.

food.title: Eat before or after on the avenues
food.p1: There is no dining on the esplanade itself. Plan coffee or lunch in the surrounding avenues or back toward the medina and ville nouvelle.
food.p2: Treat Hassan Tower as a monument stop, not a food stop.
food.li1: Café on the main avenues nearby
food.li2: Lunch in the ville nouvelle after the visit
food.li3: Water and sun protection on the open esplanade
food.li4: Combine with mausoleum before seeking a restaurant
food.li5: Avoid leaving bags unattended while photographing

tips.title: Practical Tips for Visiting Hassan Tower

1.title: Read the unfinished plan on the ground
1.desc: Walk the full rectangle of columns before focusing only on the tower. The empty footprint explains the ambition better than any single photo of the minaret. Closed shoes help on uneven stone.

2.title: Coordinate with the Mausoleum schedule
2.desc: The two sites sit together. Modest dress is essential if you enter the mausoleum. Guard ceremonies and peak tour times can cluster midday — arrive earlier for a calmer esplanade.

3.title: Wind, sun and open space
3.desc: There is little shade on the esplanade. Bring water, a hat in summer, and a light layer when the Atlantic wind picks up. Keep valuables close; it is a major tourist node with pickpocket risk in dense groups.

rabat_mausoleum_page.name: Mohammed V Mausoleum
rabat_mausoleum_page.hero_subtitle: White marble, royal guards and a quiet hall beside Hassan Tower.

overview.title: Modern memory next to medieval ambition
overview.p1: The Mausoleum of Mohammed V holds the tombs of Mohammed V and Hassan II in a white marble pavilion that contrasts with the ruined columns of Hassan Tower outside. It is formal, ceremonial and one of the capital’s most visited interiors.
overview.p2: Inside, zellij, carved plaster and the guarded silence set a different tone from the open esplanade. Photography rules and dress expectations are stricter than at many outdoor sites.
overview.p3: Plan it as a short, focused visit after or before the tower. The combination is the classic Rabat “power and memory” stop on the Bouregreg side of the city.

moods.subtitle: Three ways to experience the mausoleum

q1.question: Is entry free?
q1.answer: Access is generally free; follow current rules at the entrance for bags and dress.

q2.question: What should I wear?
q2.answer: Modest clothing covering shoulders and knees is expected. Remove hats inside if asked.

q3.question: Can I take photos?
q3.answer: Rules can restrict photography inside — follow signs and staff instructions.

q4.question: How long is the visit?
q4.answer: Twenty to forty minutes for most visitors.

q5.question: Is it open during prayer times?
q5.answer: Hours can vary on religious days; check locally if your visit falls on a holiday.

food.title: No food inside — plan around the visit
food.p1: Nothing is sold inside the mausoleum. Eat and drink on the avenues before or after, combined with your Hassan Tower stop.
food.p2: Keep bottles out of the formal hall.

food.li2: Lunch after both tower and mausoleum

tips.title: Practical Tips for Visiting the Mohammed V Mausoleum

1.title: Dress and bags before you reach the door
1.desc: Cover shoulders and knees; carry a light scarf if needed. Large bags may be checked or restricted. Sorting this at the hotel saves awkward moments at the entrance.

2.title: Quiet is part of the architecture
2.desc: Keep voices low, phones silent, and move with the flow of visitors. The hall is designed for formal respect — treat it closer to a ceremonial space than a museum gallery.

3.title: Do tower and mausoleum as one block
3.desc: Arrive once, see both, then leave for food or the next neighbourhood. Splitting them with a long lunch in between means a second security and heat cycle on the open esplanade.

rabat_chellah_page.name: Chellah
rabat_chellah_page.hero_subtitle: Roman ruins and Merinid walls where storks nest above the Bouregreg marsh.

overview.title: Two layers of history in one hillside enclosure
overview.p1: Chellah (ancient Sala) wraps Roman remains and a Merinid necropolis inside later walls. Storks nest on the ruins; the site feels half archaeological park, half garden above the river wetlands.
overview.p2: You walk from the gate down through tombs, minaret ruins and stone foundations, with more space and fewer coaches than the kasbah at peak hour. It is one of Rabat’s best places to slow down.
overview.p3: Late afternoon light is kind to the stone and the birds. Bring water; shade is partial. Combine with a quiet taxi ride rather than forcing it into a rushed monument checklist.

moods.subtitle: Three ways to experience Chellah

q1.question: Is there an entry fee?
q1.answer: Yes — a modest ticket is usual at the entrance; keep small notes ready.

q2.question: How long do I need?
q2.answer: About one to two hours for a calm walk through the main areas.

q3.question: Are the paths difficult?
q3.answer: Some slopes and uneven stones — closed shoes recommended; not ideal for limited mobility without help.

q4.question: Best time for storks?
q4.answer: Nesting season varies; birds are often visible even outside peak breeding months.

q5.question: Far from the centre?
q5.answer: A short taxi ride from the ville nouvelle or Hassan area — not a long excursion.

food.title: Picnic shade or return to town
food.p1: Facilities inside are limited. Bring water; plan a proper meal back in the city after your visit.
food.p2: Chellah is for walking and looking, not for restaurant rows.

food.li2: Light snack only if you need it
food.li4: No expectation of a full café terrace inside
food.li5: Combine with a ville nouvelle meal the same afternoon

tips.title: Practical Tips for Visiting Chellah

1.title: Give it a full hour minimum
1.desc: Chellah is not a ten-minute photo stop. Walk the lower ruins, pause at the stork nests, and let the site’s double history (Roman / Merinid) register. Rushing only collects dust and similar pictures.

2.title: Shoes, sun and slopes
2.desc: Paths include uneven stone and gentle descents toward the marsh side. Closed shoes with grip matter. Summer midday is harsh — morning or late afternoon is more comfortable and better for photographs.

3.title: Taxi in, calm out
3.desc: Agree a taxi price from Hassan Tower or your hotel, or use a ride app where available. Pairing Chellah with the kasbah the same morning is possible but dense; many travellers prefer Chellah as a separate, slower half-day.

rabat_medina_page.name: Rabat Medina
rabat_medina_page.hero_subtitle: A compact medina between the kasbah and the ville nouvelle — easier to navigate than Fez, still fully Moroccan.

overview.title: Markets, walls and everyday capital life
overview.p1: Rabat’s medina is smaller and less labyrinthine than Fez or Marrakech, which makes it ideal for a first medina experience. You get souk streets, food stalls and residential life without the same intensity of touts.
overview.p2: Walk from the kasbah edge toward the central lanes, notice the scale of the walls, and use it as a link between the historic core and the French-planned avenues of the ville nouvelle.
overview.p3: Morning is best for shopping energy; evening brings a different food rhythm. It is a place to buy spices, have juice and watch ordinary Rabat move — not only a monument corridor.

moods.subtitle: Three ways to experience the medina

1.title: Food and craft lanes
1.desc: Spices, olives and everyday shopping streets.

3.desc: How the capital’s layers connect on foot.

q1.question: Is the medina safe to walk?
q1.answer: Yes in normal tourist hours — use usual city awareness with bags and phones in crowded lanes.

q2.question: Do I need a guide?
q2.answer: Not required for a first look; a guide helps if you want craft workshops or deeper history.

q3.question: How does it compare to Fez?
q3.answer: Smaller, flatter in parts, easier to exit toward the ville nouvelle — less overwhelming for a first medina.

q4.question: Best for shopping?
q4.answer: Foodstuffs, simple crafts and everyday goods; luxury craft hunting is stronger in Fez or Marrakech.

q5.question: Evening atmosphere?
q5.answer: Livelier food streets; some lanes quiet down earlier than in larger tourist medinas.

food.title: Juice, grilled snacks and simple restaurants
food.p1: The medina is one of the easiest places in Rabat to eat casually: fresh juice, grilled meats, and small restaurants aimed at locals and visitors.
food.p2: Follow busy tables rather than empty tourist menus on side corners.
food.li1: Fresh orange juice on a main lane
food.li2: Grilled brochettes at a busy stall
food.li3: Harira or snack soups where locals sit
food.li5: Save a longer dinner for the ville nouvelle if you want more choice

tips.title: Practical Tips for Visiting Rabat Medina

1.title: Use it as a connector, not only a destination
1.desc: Enter from the kasbah side, cross toward a gate that faces the ville nouvelle, and you learn the city’s layout while shopping. Getting “a little lost” here is safer and shorter than in Fez’s deeper alleys.

2.title: Money and bargaining
2.desc: Carry small notes for juice and snacks. Bargain politely on crafts; fixed-price food is usually labelled or obvious. Avoid following strangers to “special” shops far off your route.

3.title: Heat and timing
3.desc: Covered lanes help at midday, but summer still drains energy — do the medina in the morning, monuments that need open-sky walking later or earlier. Keep a tram or taxi plan for the return with bags.

rabat_gardens_page.name: Andalusian Gardens
rabat_gardens_page.hero_subtitle: Shaded paths and fountains beside the Kasbah of the Udayas.

overview.title: A green pause under the kasbah walls
overview.p1: The Andalusian Gardens sit next to the Kasbah of the Udayas — formal paths, citrus and shade that offer a break from white walls and Atlantic glare.
overview.p2: It is not a vast botanical destination; it is a designed garden that completes a kasbah morning. Families and photographers use it for softer light and quieter benches.
overview.p3: Visit after the kasbah lanes or before the river viewpoint. Ticket rules can differ from the free residential streets — check at the entrance.

q1.question: Is there a ticket?
q1.answer: Often a modest fee separate from walking the kasbah streets — confirm at the gate.

q2.question: How long do I need?
q2.answer: Thirty to sixty minutes is enough for most visits.

q3.question: Good with children?
q3.answer: Yes — open paths and shade; still supervise near any water features.

q4.question: Best time?
q4.answer: Late morning after the kasbah, or midday when you need shade most.

q5.question: Can I picnic?
q5.answer: Follow posted rules; many visitors simply sit on benches with water, not full picnics.

food.title: Tea after the garden, not inside
food.p1: Eat and drink outside the garden perimeter — kasbah cafés and medina lanes are minutes away.
food.p2: Keep the garden for walking and rest, not for meals.
food.li2: Tea on a kasbah terrace afterward
food.li3: Medina snack on the way out
food.li4: No restaurant row inside the garden

tips.title: Practical Tips for Visiting the Andalusian Gardens

1.title: Treat it as the kasbah’s cooler room
1.desc: Do the bright lanes and viewpoint first or second, and use the garden when you need shade. It is small enough that a slow loop is better than racing every path for photos.

2.title: Tickets and opening rhythm
2.desc: Confirm fee and closing time at the entrance — garden hours can differ from the always-open residential streets of the kasbah. Last entry matters if you arrive late afternoon.

3.title: Photography without blocking paths
3.desc: Popular corners fill with posed shoots. Step aside, keep paths clear, and save drone ideas for elsewhere — this is a compact public garden beside homes.

rabat_beach_page.name: Rabat Beach & Corniche
rabat_beach_page.hero_subtitle: Atlantic air on the capital’s edge — walks, surf energy and sunset light.

overview.title: Sea front without leaving the capital
overview.p1: Rabat’s beach and corniche stretch along the Atlantic side of the city — a place for evening walks, weekend families and a different pace from the medina. It is not a tropical resort strip; it is an urban ocean edge with wind and real city life.
overview.p2: Come for the breeze after a day of monuments, for a run or for coffee facing the water. Swimming conditions depend on flags, currents and season — respect local advice.
overview.p3: Sunset pulls a crowd; early morning is quieter. Link it with the kasbah viewpoint in your mental map: river mouth one side, open Atlantic the other.

moods.title: What to See on Rabat Beach & Corniche
moods.subtitle: Three ways to experience the seafront

1.title: Corniche promenade
1.desc: Ocean air after stone and souks.

2.title: Sunset on the Atlantic
2.desc: The capital’s evening reset.

3.title: Weekend rhythm
3.desc: Families, joggers and surf culture nearby.

q1.question: Is it safe to swim?
q1.answer: Follow local flags and advice — Atlantic currents can be strong. When in doubt, stay on the sand.

q2.question: Far from the medina?
q2.answer: A short taxi or a longer walk depending on which stretch of corniche you choose.

q3.question: Good for children?
q3.answer: Yes for sand and walks; supervise closely near the water.

q4.question: Facilities?
q4.answer: Vary by section — some cafés and services, not a continuous resort strip.

q5.question: Best time?
q5.answer: Late afternoon and evening for atmosphere; morning for quieter walks.

food.title: Corniche cafés and seafood nearby
food.p1: Cafés and simple restaurants along parts of the seafront serve drinks and seafood. Quality varies — busy local places are usually a better sign than empty tourist terraces.
food.p2: For a serious fish meal, ask your hotel for a current recommendation rather than trusting the first menu on the windiest corner.
food.li3: Ice cream on a family evening walk
food.li4: Water and windbreaker in cooler months
food.li5: Dinner back in the ville nouvelle if you want more choice

tips.title: Practical Tips for Visiting Rabat Beach & Corniche

1.title: Wind is part of the deal
1.desc: The Atlantic here is often breezy. Bring a light layer even in seasons that feel warm inland. Sand and salt stick to camera gear — protect lenses if you shoot at sunset.

2.title: Swim only when conditions allow
2.desc: This is not a swimming-pool coastline. Read flags, watch locals, and skip the water if you are unsure. The value of the stop is often the walk and the air, not a long swim.

3.title: Time it as a counterweight to monuments
3.desc: After Chellah or Hassan Tower, the corniche resets the day. Pair sunset here with an earlier indoor or medina slot so you are not inventing a fourth monument at dusk.

rabat_marina_page.hero_subtitle: Modern waterfront between Rabat and Salé — cafés, boats and a different face of the capital.

overview.title: The river city reinvented along the Bouregreg
overview.p1: The Bouregreg Marina area shows contemporary Rabat: promenades, restaurants, cultural venues and boats against the backdrop of two historic cities facing each other across the river.
overview.p2: It is a contrast to the kasbah and Chellah — useful when you want a polished evening, a longer dinner, or a sense of how the capital invests in its river edge.
overview.p3: Come at golden hour for reflections, or after dark when terraces fill. It pairs well with a daytime monument schedule rather than replacing it.

moods.subtitle: Three ways to experience the marina

q1.question: Is it free to walk?
q1.answer: The public promenades are free; restaurants and venues have their own pricing.

q2.question: How do I get there?
q2.answer: Taxi or ride from central Rabat; some visitors combine with Salé on the other bank.

q3.question: Good for dinner?
q3.answer: Yes — one of the easier areas for a longer, modern restaurant evening.

q4.question: Family friendly?
q4.answer: Yes for walks and open space; watch children near the water edge.

q5.question: Worth it on a short trip?
q5.answer: If you have an evening free after monuments — less essential than the kasbah or Chellah on a single-day dash.

food.title: Marina restaurants and café terraces
food.p1: This is one of the best zones in Rabat for a sit-down contemporary meal with a view. Menus lean international and Moroccan-modern; prices sit above medina stalls.
food.p2: Book ahead on weekends if you want a specific terrace at sunset.
food.li3: Coffee with a river view by day
food.li4: Budget a higher bill than medina snacks
food.li5: Combine with a slow walk after eating

tips.title: Practical Tips for Visiting Bouregreg Marina

1.title: Use it as an evening chapter
1.desc: Monuments work better in daylight. Save the marina for when you want atmosphere, dinner and a sense of modern Rabat without another ticket queue. One strong evening here beats a rushed midday photo stop.

2.title: Transport both ways
2.desc: Agree taxi return plans or check ride-app coverage before you settle into a long meal. The area is pleasant, but walking back to every hotel neighbourhood is not realistic after dark.

3.title: Balance old and new in your story of the city
3.desc: If your only images are marina lights, you have missed the capital. If you never see the river’s modern edge, you miss how Rabat presents itself today. Aim for both across a two-day stay.

rabat_museum_page.name: Musée Mohammed VI
rabat_museum_page.hero_subtitle: Contemporary and modern art in a landmark building of the capital.

overview.title: Art indoors when the monuments can wait
overview.p1: The Mohammed VI Museum of Modern and Contemporary Art (MMVI) gives Rabat a major cultural indoor stop — rotating exhibitions, Moroccan modern art and a building that is part of the visit itself.
overview.p2: Use it when you want air-conditioning, context and a break from open-air ruins. It is especially useful in summer heat or on a day when you have already walked the kasbah and Chellah.
overview.p3: Check current exhibitions before you go; the permanent story of Moroccan modernism pairs well with temporary shows. Plan one to two hours.

moods.title: What to See at Musée Mohammed VI
moods.subtitle: Three ways to experience the museum

1.title: Modern Moroccan works
1.desc: Painting and media beyond the tourist craft narrative.

2.desc: The museum structure as part of the capital’s cultural statement.

3.title: Indoor contrast
3.desc: Quiet rooms after bright outdoor sites.

q1.question: Is there an entry fee?
q1.answer: Yes — standard museum ticket; check for temporary exhibition surcharges.

q2.question: How long do I need?
q2.answer: One to two hours depending on exhibitions and your pace.

q3.question: English labels?
q3.answer: Labelling varies by show; the visual work carries much of the experience.

q4.question: Bags and photos?
q4.answer: Follow cloakroom and photo rules at the entrance — they can change by exhibition.

q5.question: Worth it on a short Rabat trip?
q5.answer: Yes if you care about art or need an indoor slot; skip only if you have a single day for outdoor icons alone.

food.title: Café at the museum or nearby avenues
food.p1: Museum visits pair naturally with a café stop. Check whether the on-site café is open; otherwise the ville nouvelle avenues nearby have plenty of options.

tips.title: Practical Tips for Visiting Musée Mohammed VI

1.title: Check the exhibition calendar first
1.desc: A strong temporary show can be the reason to go; a turnover week might mean partial closures. Five minutes on the museum’s current programme saves disappointment at the desk.

2.title: Place it in a heat or fatigue slot
2.desc: After Chellah’s slopes or a full medina morning, an indoor museum restores energy. Avoid putting it first if morning light on the kasbah is your priority.

3.title: Combine with ville nouvelle, not with another ticket rush
3.desc: Leave time to sit with a few works rather than collecting another stamp. Pair with avenue walking or a calm lunch; do not force Hassan Tower, Chellah and MMVI into the same breathless afternoon.

seo.og_title: Merzouga Travel Guide | Erg Chebbi & Desert Camps | MoroccoTripMap
seo.og_description: Dunes, camel treks and desert camps — a complete guide to Merzouga and Erg Chebbi.

hero.title: Merzouga
hero.subtitle: Golden dunes, camel treks and nights under a desert sky at the edge of Erg Chebbi.

overview.title: Why Visit Merzouga
overview.p1: Merzouga is the classic gateway to Erg Chebbi, one of Morocco’s most photogenic dune fields. Travellers come for sunset camel rides, overnight camps and the silence of the Sahara after dark.
overview.p2: The village itself is small; the experience is the erg, the camps and short side trips to Khamlia, Dayet Srji and Rissani. Plan at least one night in the dunes if you can.

places.title: Must-Visit Places in Merzouga
places.subtitle: Dunes, camel treks, camps and the stops that define the desert gateway.

erg.title: Erg Chebbi
erg.desc: Vast golden dunes rising above Merzouga — the heart of every Sahara visit here.

village.title: Merzouga Village
village.desc: Small desert gateway with hotels, cafés and the trailhead to the erg.

camel.title: Camel Trek
camel.desc: Classic camel ride into the dunes at sunset or sunrise — the signature Merzouga experience.

camp.title: Desert Camp
camp.desc: Overnight in a Berber-style camp under the stars — dinner, drums and dune silence.

khamlia.title: Khamlia
khamlia.desc: Desert village known for Gnawa music, tea and warm hospitality near the dunes.

dayet.title: Dayet Srji
dayet.desc: Seasonal lake at the foot of the dunes — flamingos when water is present after rains.

rissani.title: Rissani
rissani.desc: Historic market town — souk days, kasbahs and the Moulay Ali Cherif mausoleum.

hassilabied.title: Hassilabied
hassilabied.desc: Quiet village on the edge of the erg — hotels with dune views and a calmer base.

fossils.title: Fossil Workshops
fossils.desc: Workshops and shops with trilobites and polished fossils from the Erfoud region.

taourirt.title: Erg Chebbi
taourirt.desc: Iconic mud-brick kasbah in town — restored sections, lanes and classic desert-edge views.

studios.title: Camel trek
studios.desc: One of the world’s largest film studios — sets from biblical epics to desert blockbusters.

ait.title: Erg Chebbi
ait.desc: UNESCO ksar of earthen houses — the most famous fortified village near Merzouga.

tifoultoute.title: Kasbah Hassilabied
tifoultoute.desc: Hilltop kasbah a short drive from town — quieter than Merzouga village, strong views.

museum.title: Musée du Cinéma
museum.desc: Film props, sets and the story of Merzouga as Morocco’s Hollywood of the desert.

fint.title: Oasis de Dayet Srji
fint.desc: Palm oasis in a rocky valley south of town — quiet walks and local life.

skoura.title: Rissani
skoura.desc: Vast palm grove and kasbahs east of Merzouga — slower pace on the Road of the Kasbahs.

cla.title: CLA Studios
cla.desc: Another major studio complex near town — film sets open to visitors when not in production.

lake.title: Lac El Mansour Eddahbi
lake.desc: Reservoir near Merzouga — water, birds and a different landscape from the dry kasbahs.

itinerary.title: Suggested 3-Day Itinerary
itinerary.subtitle: Dunes, a night in camp, and the villages around Erg Chebbi.

day1.title: Erg Chebbi & Town
day1.desc: Morning at Erg Chebbi, afternoon Cinema Museum or Camel Trek, evening in town.

day2.title: Erg Chebbi
day2.desc: Full morning and afternoon at the UNESCO ksar; optional stop at Hassilabied on the way back.

day3.title: Oasis, Rissani or Desert Road
day3.desc: Dayet Srji oasis or Rissani palm grove, or start a multi-day trip toward Zagora or Merzouga.

detailed_itinerary.day1_md: Drive or walk to the edge of Erg Chebbi. Climb a dune for the first panoramic view before the heat peaks.
detailed_itinerary.day1_ad: Return to the village for lunch, fossil shops, and time to arrange your camel trek and camp.
detailed_itinerary.day1_ed: Watch sunset from a dune ridge, then dinner at your hotel or a village restaurant.
detailed_itinerary.day2_md: A quiet morning in the village or Hassilabied; rest before the afternoon trek.
detailed_itinerary.day2_a: Afternoon — Camel trek into Erg Chebbi
detailed_itinerary.day2_ad: Depart as arranged with your camp: camel trek into the dunes toward your overnight stay.
detailed_itinerary.day2_ed: Berber dinner, drums and stars; sleep in a tent or camp with optional sunrise climb.
detailed_itinerary.day3_md: Climb for sunrise, breakfast at camp, then camel or 4x4 back to the village.
detailed_itinerary.day3_ad: Gnawa music and tea in Khamlia, or Rissani’s souk and Moulay Ali Cherif mausoleum.
detailed_itinerary.day3_ed: Quiet dinner before onward travel toward Erfoud, Tinghir or Ouarzazate.

tips.title: Practical Tips for Visiting Merzouga
tips.subtitle: Desert heat, cash and camp choices matter more here than in the imperial cities.

cash.title: Cash & ATMs
cash.desc: Bring enough dirhams. ATMs are limited; camps and small shops often prefer cash.

shoes.title: Shoes & sun
shoes.desc: Closed shoes for dunes, scarf or hat, strong sunscreen. Nights can be cold even after hot days.

stay.title: Hotel vs camp
stay.desc: Sleep one night in a desert camp if possible, and keep a village hotel for arrival/departure flexibility.

guide.title: Book camps wisely
guide.desc: Agree inclusions (camel, dinner, breakfast, 4x4) in advance. Standards vary from basic to luxury.

1.title: Heat and sun
1.desc: Merzouga is dry and can be very hot. High SPF, hat, water — especially at Erg Chebbi and outdoor studios.

2.title: Erg Chebbi by taxi or tour
2.desc: Agree a round-trip price including waiting time. Half a day is realistic from town.

3.title: Studio access
3.desc: Atlas and CLA opening depends on filming. Confirm the same morning.

transport.title: Getting there
transport.desc: Airport OZZ, buses and shared taxis from Marrakech via Tizi n’Tichka, or private transfer.

bargain.title: Shopping
bargain.desc: Souvenir stalls at Erg Chebbi expect bargaining. Stay polite and walk away if needed.

water.title: Desert road safety
water.desc: For multi-day desert trips, use reputable operators; roads and dunes need experience.

daytrips.title: Best Day Trips from Merzouga
daytrips.subtitle: Short hops that pair well with a dunes stay.

erfoud.title: Erfoud
erfoud.desc: Fossil town and market on the approach to Merzouga.

tinghir.title: Tinghir & Todra
tinghir.desc: Gorges and palm valley on the route back toward the High Atlas.

rissani.title: Rissani souk
rissani.desc: Weekly market atmosphere and historic gates near Merzouga.

ouarzazate.title: Toward Ouarzazate
ouarzazate.desc: Multi-day route via Draa or Dades if continuing west.

rabat.title: Zagora & Draa Valley
rabat.desc: South into the Draa — palm groves, kasbahs and the road toward the desert.

taghazout.title: Merzouga dunes
taghazout.desc: Multi-day classic toward Erg Chebbi — best as overnight, not a rushed day trip.

mohammedia.title: Dadès & Todra
mohammedia.desc: Gorges and valley scenery on the road east — often part of a desert circuit.

azemmour.title: Marrakech (return)
azemmour.desc: Many travellers return via the High Atlas Tizi n’Tichka pass.

zagora.title: Erfoud
zagora.desc: Fossil town and market on the approach to Merzouga.

q1.question: How many nights should I spend in Merzouga?
q1.answer: One night in a desert camp plus a night in the village is ideal. Two camp nights suit photographers and slower travellers.

q2.question: When is the best time to visit?
q2.answer: October–April for milder days. Summer is extremely hot; winter nights are cold on the dunes.

q3.question: Do I need to book a camel trek in advance?
q3.answer: In high season yes, especially for overnight camps. In quieter months you can often arrange on arrival through your hotel.

q4.question: Is Merzouga only for desert trips?
q4.answer: It is the main gateway, but kasbahs and studios are worth a stop even without dunes.

seo.og_title: Meknes Travel Guide | Imperial Gates & Roman Volubilis | MoroccoTripMap
seo.og_description: Imperial Meknes, Roman Volubilis and the holy town of Moulay Idriss — gates, granaries and a calmer medina than Fez.

meknes_page.hero_subtitle: Bab Mansour, Place el-Hedim, Heri es-Souani and the road to Roman Volubilis — the imperial city that still feels local.

overview.title: Meknes: Imperial Gates, Granaries and the Road to Volubilis
overview.p1: Meknes is the imperial city of Moulay Ismail: monumental gates, vast granaries and a medina that is easier to walk than Fez. Place el-Hedim and Bab Mansour set the scene; Heri es-Souani shows the scale of the sultan’s logistics. It is also the natural base for Volubilis and Moulay Idriss Zerhoun without the day-trip rush from farther cities.
overview.p2: Two full days cover the imperial core and the medina; a third day fits the Roman ruins and the holy hillside town. Stays cluster near the medina and Ville Nouvelle — practical if you arrive by train and want both history and calm evenings.

itinerary.title: Suggested 3-Day Itinerary
itinerary.subtitle: Imperial Meknes, then Volubilis and Moulay Idriss without rushing.
itinerary.day1: Day 1 — Place el-Hedim, Bab Mansour, medina & Dar Jamai
itinerary.day2: Day 2 — Mausoleum, Heri es-Souani & Medersa Bou Inania

detailed_itinerary.day1_md: Start on Place el-Hedim while the square is still quiet. Face Bab Mansour, walk the gate details, then enter the medina lanes for a first orientation and coffee.
detailed_itinerary.day1_ad: Continue through the medina souks toward Dar Jamai Museum. Keep the pace slow — Meknes rewards looking up at woodwork and courtyards more than ticking boxes.
detailed_itinerary.day1_ed: Return to Place el-Hedim for sunset light on the gate. Dinner near the square or in a medina riad restaurant.
detailed_itinerary.day2_md: Visit the Mausoleum of Moulay Ismail early (check opening rules and dress). Then head to Heri es-Souani for the granaries and stables while the light is still soft.
detailed_itinerary.day2_ad: Medersa Bou Inania for tilework and quiet courtyards, then free time in Ville Nouvelle or a second medina loop for crafts and olives.
detailed_itinerary.day2_ed: Rooftop or simple grill near the medina. Rest early if tomorrow is Volubilis.
detailed_itinerary.day3_md: Drive or grand taxi to Volubilis. Walk the forum, triumphal arch and mosaics before the heat builds.
detailed_itinerary.day3_ad: Continue to Moulay Idriss Zerhoun. Climb to a viewpoint, respect the sacred character of the town, then return to Meknes.
detailed_itinerary.day3_ed: Last evening in Meknes — Place el-Hedim once more or a calm dinner before a train to Fès or Rabat.
